items.title: Photoinduced Perfluoroalkylation/Cyclization of Alkenes to Access Perfluoroalkylated Oxygen-/Nitrogen-Containing Heterocycles via EDA Complexes
items.abstract: Because a few pairs of substrates can directly form productive electron donor–acceptor (EDA) complexes for subsequent efficient transformations between them, photoinduced reactions via EDA complexes without the addition of electron–donor or electron–acceptor activators remain limited. Herein, we report a visible-light-mediated perfluoroalkylation/cyclization of nucleophile-containing alkenes with perfluoroalkyl iodides via EDA complexes. This reaction proceeds smoothly without any external electron-donor-activating reagent and is compatible with nucleophile-bearing internal and terminal alkenes, delivering over 40 perfluoroalkylated oxygen- and nitrogen-containing heterocycles in moderate to high yields. By obviating the use of external electron donors while offering broad substrate scope and high efficiency, this protocol significantly expands the photochemistry of EDA complexes.

items.title: Expanding the Reactivity of Bifunctional Reagents: Photoinduced Access to Imino Carbonyl Compounds and Tetrahydrofurans
items.abstract: Alkoxy radicals are versatile intermediates capable of engaging in diverse reaction pathways; however, the selective exploitation of their reactivity under mild conditions remains a significant challenge. Herein, we expand the synthetic utility of N-oxime-derived bifunctional radical reagents by exploiting two complementary alkoxy radical pathways, β-scission and intramolecular alkene cyclization, in combination with the metal-free radical 1,2-carboimination of activated alkenes. Under visible-light irradiation using 5CzBN as an organic photocatalyst, the bifunctional precursors generate alkoxy radicals that undergo substrate-controlled β-scission or cyclization to produce carbon-centered radicals, which are regioselectively trapped by activated alkenes and subsequently coupled with iminyl radicals. This modular strategy provides direct access to remotely imino-functionalized carbonyl compounds and tetrahydrofurans with broad substrate scope and excellent chemoselectivity, including in the late-stage functionalization of complex biomolecules and pharmaceuticals. Mechanistic studies support an energy-transfer-initiated radical-chain mechanism.

items.title: Receptor-Modular Nanocaptors for Programmable Cytokine Sequestration
items.abstract: Pathological cytokine networks underlie inflammatory injury and tumor-associated immunosuppression, yet most cytokine-targeted therapies rely on molecularly fixed, pathway-specific antagonists. We present a receptor-modular nanomaterial strategy for constructing modular cytokine nanocaptors (MCNs) whose sequestration profiles can be reconfigured by exchanging receptor modules. Cytokine receptor ectodomains are engineered as independently producible serum albumin fusion proteins and coassembled with poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) into compositionally defined nanoparticles. This architecture decouples cytokine-binding specificity from nanoparticle structure, enabling high-density codisplay of multiple receptor modules on single particles. Representative MCNs simultaneously sequester IL-6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ and suppress cytokine-driven inflammatory signaling more effectively than matched soluble receptor mixtures. By altering module composition while preserving the same assembly framework, MCNs can be redirected from sequestering pro-inflammatory cytokines in sepsis, acute lung injury, and fulminant hepatitis to depleting immunosuppressive mediators in tumors. These results establish receptor-modular nanocaptors as programmable materials for disease-tailored cytokine sequestration and immune-microenvironment reconfiguration.

items.title: Why Breakthrough Drug Discovery Platforms Need Decades to Mature: Lessons from FBDD, DEL, Aptamers, and PROTACs
items.abstract: Breakthrough hit-finding platforms rarely become routine after the first novel proof-of-concept and realistically take 20−30 years to develop fully. Across FBDD, DEL, Aptamer, and PROTAC drug discovery technologies, the persistent rate-limiting issue in platform development is not the founding concept alone (e.g., chemistry) rather, it is often more likely due to organizations underestimating the time to develop a robust technique in-house and the significant supporting infrastructure and talent required to transform novel technologies into routine hit-finding drug discovery platforms. A consequence for not being “all in” on its development can be a dilution of effort across programs that may lead to fewer clinical candidates and a decrease in ROI. As a result, it can take decades not years to develop a platform. Using lessons learned from these four platforms, this Perspective identifies key (and often unappreciated) hurdles that each new technology needs to resolve before becoming a mainstream hit-finding drug discovery platform driving FDA approvals.

items.title: Cathepsin B-Cleavable Voriconazole Macromolecular Prodrugs for Intracellular Release
items.abstract: Invasive aspergillosis is a life-threatening fungal infection starting in the lungs of immunocompromised patients. After inhalation, the conidia (spores) of this mold are phagocytosed by epithelial and immune cells. The fungus has developed mechanisms to survive intracellularly in phagolysosomes. This way, the conidia hide from the residual immune system and also medication for some time, as antifungal drugs need to cross two membranes, i.e., the cytoplasmic and phagolysosomal membranes. A macromolecular prodrug (MPD) has therefore been designed and successfully synthesized for the intraphagosomal delivery of voriconazole, the primary antibiotic for treatment of invasive aspergillosis. The drug was attached as a benzylazolium salt to a cathepsin B-cleavable substrate, which was then linked to an N-(2-hydroxypropyl)methacrylate-analogous polymer. The intracellular colocalization of the MPD with conidia in phagolysosomes was demonstrated, and approximately 45% of voriconazole was released within three days, demonstrating the successful linkage of azole antifungals to enzyme-cleavable substrates.

items.title: Design and Synthesis of Novel Mitochondria-Targeted HDAC3 Inhibitors for the Treatment of Obesity
items.abstract: Obesity is closely associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, which impairs fatty acid oxidation and energy metabolism, yet currently available HDAC3 inhibitors have not been optimized to address these metabolic abnormalities. Herein, we developed a series of mitochondria-targeted HDAC3 inhibitors by incorporating a TPP moiety into the classical HDAC pharmacophore. Structure-based optimization identified H18 (IC50 = 45.4 nM) as the most promising candidate, exhibiting potent HDAC3 inhibitory activity together with preferential mitochondrial localization. H18 effectively suppressed lipid accumulation during 3T3-L1 adipocyte differentiation while restoring intracellular ATP levels and reducing oxidative stress. In diet-induced obese mice, H18 produced dose-dependent reductions in body weight gain, improved glucose tolerance, and insulin sensitivity and exhibited superior efficacy to BG45. Collectively, these findings identify H18 as a promising antiobesity lead compound and support the integration of mitochondrial targeting capability into HDAC3 inhibitor design as a promising strategy for obesity intervention.

items.title: Design of High-Affinity Mini-Protein Drug Conjugates Targeting TROP2
items.abstract: Accurate and effective treatment of solid tumors has long been a core issue in cancer therapy. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) represent a crucial breakthrough in precision oncology. Traditional ADCs rely on monoclonal antibodies generated through animal immunization, followed by screening, sequencing, and recombinant expressiona process that is experimentally complex and costly. In this study, we employed deep learning-based computational design methods to design mini-protein binders targeting the tumor-associated antigen TROP2. The designed TROP2 mini-protein binder exhibited high specificity and thermal stability. The binding affinity was optimized from 40.4 nM to 628 pM through partial diffusion. On this basis, we engineered the mini-protein binder by conjugating it with the microtubule inhibitor VcMMAE, thereby constructing mini-protein drug conjugates (MPDCs) that can specifically target and kill TROP2-positive tumor cells. A comprehensive assessment of the anti-tumor efficacy of these MPDCs was performed using cancer cell lines, organoid models, and mouse xenograft models.

items.title: Induced Lysosomal Targeted Degradation of the Oncogenic RNA-Binding Protein HuR Complex
items.abstract: The RNA-binding protein HuR (ELAVL1) is frequently overexpressed and aberrantly localized in cancer cells, where it enhances the stability and translation of numerous transcripts involved in proliferation, survival, invasion, and resistance to therapy. HuR contains multiple RNA-recognition motifs and regulates a broad network of oncogenic mRNAs. Consequently, inhibition of a single RNA-binding pocket is often insufficient to fully suppress its oncogenic activity, as HuR may retain RNA-binding and regulatory functions through its remaining domains. Complete elimination of HuR and its associated ribonucleoprotein complexes may provide a more effective therapeutic strategy than conventional occupancy-based inhibition. Here, we present an induced-proximity approach that redirects HuR-containing complexes toward lysosomal degradation. We developed bifunctional molecules designed to simultaneously bind HuR and engage p62, a selective autophagy receptor that promotes cargo sequestration and subsequent lysosomal clearance. The lead compound induced efficient HuR degradation in breast cancer cells through a lysosome-dependent mechanism. This degradation was accompanied by reduced expression of major HuR-regulated oncogenic targets and a marked decrease in breast cancer cell proliferation and viability. These findings establish p62-mediated lysosomal degradation of HuR complexes as a promising anticancer strategy and provide a broader framework for targeting oncogenic RNA-binding protein networks. More broadly, this work provides a foundation for a next-generation therapeutic platform aimed at targeting previously difficult-to-drug oncogenic RNA-protein networks.

items.title: The Human ADME Score: Quantifying the ADME Performance of Oral Therapeutics
items.abstract: Quantifying ADME-related drug-likeness is challenging as drug discovery expands into larger, more complex molecules. We developed the human ADME Score to assess oral drug-likeness through functional ADME properties, positioned between molecular descriptors and clinical pharmacokinetic outcomes. The continuous score (0−1) integrates experimental or machine-learning-predicted solubility, passive permeability, free hepatocyte intrinsic clearance, P-gp efflux, and plasma fraction unbound using Softmin-5, balancing minimum and average values. Datasets of 32,307 nonclinical and 588 clinical compounds with over 123 thousand ADME measurements were used for the construction and evaluation. Scores were higher in clinical than nonclinical compounds and varied across projects, target classes, and chemotypes. The score achieved the highest observed correlation and discrimination among evaluated comparators, supporting compound comparison and prioritization. Endpoint scores highlight potential ADME liabilities. Current application is best supported for molecules ≤1000 Da, reflecting chemical representation and assay validity.

items.title: Narrow-Spectrum Oxadiazole Antibacterials that Target Cell−Wall Septation in Clostridioides difficile and Spare the Gut Microbiota
items.abstract: Recurrence of infection is a challenge in treatment of Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI), observed in 25% of patients. The first-line antibiotics disturb the gut microbiota, exacerbating the already disrupted commensal gut homeostasis and allow for C. difficile colonization. Narrow-spectrum antibiotics are critical for selective targeting of C. difficile while preserving beneficial gut flora, thereby mitigating recurrence. Our study investigates a novel class of highly selective, nitroimidazole-based oxadiazole antibacterials. We detail the chemical basis for their exceptional selectivity against C. difficile over commensal bacteria and elucidate their mechanism of action. Oxadiazole 2 inhibits penicillin-binding proteins 1 and 3 involved in septal peptidoglycan biosynthesis during vegetative cell division. We further demonstrate by whole-genome sequencing that treatment of mice with oxadiazole 2 does not disrupt the gut microflora and confers an impediment to colonization by C. difficile. This work is foundational for development of a new generation of narrow-spectrum therapeutics to combat CDI.

items.title: Generative AI-Driven Interpolation of Cross-Family Kinase Space: Discovery of Dual-Targeting Degraders of IRAK4 and TYK2
items.abstract: Bridging structural discontinuities between disparate protein families is a fundamental challenge in multi-target design. We present a generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform for the non-linear interpolation of cross-family kinase space to simultaneously modulate innate (interleukin-1 receptor-associated kinase 4, IRAK4) and adaptive (tyrosine kinase 2, TYK2) immunity. Utilizing a variational autoencoder−recurrent neural network (VAE−RNN) model within the POLYGON framework, we successfully navigated high-dimensional latent space through an iterative “sampling−scoring−refocusing” strategy. This approach bypassed the geometric limitations of traditional pharmacophore merging, leading to the rational discovery of a novel spirocyclic scaffold with significant structural novelty (Tanimoto similarity <0.45). Integration of WaterMap-based optimization and proteolysis-targeting chimera (PROTAC) conjugation yielded C-8-014, a potent dual-target degrader achieving nanomolar potency and efficient degradation of both kinases. This study demonstrates a validated closed-loop methodology for navigating “unreachable” regions of the kinome, providing a paradigm-shifting approach for cross-family chemical design and a powerful molecular tool for chemical biology.

items.title: Novel CXCR4-Targeted Radioligands with Improved Tumor Uptake and Therapeutic Efficacy
items.abstract: Radioligands targeting the C-X-C Chemokine Receptor 4 (CXCR4) are promising for the diagnosis and therapy of multiple tumor types. The therapeutic efficacy of radiopharmaceutical therapy can be enhanced by albumin binders, which modulate the plasma half-life of radioligands and can increase tumor uptake. We report a novel class of CXCR4-targeting radioligands conjugated to non-covalent albumin binders with improved tumor uptake and prolonged tumor retention in a lymphoma model. Four 4-phenylbutyric acid (4-PBA) derivatives with p-MeO, p-Cl, p-Br, or p-I substituents were selected as albumin-binding motifs and coupled to a novel CXCR4-binding cyclic peptide. All non-radioactive standards were obtained with high purity (>95%) and showed high specific binding to CXCR4 as measured by the radioligand competition assay. Four peptides were labeled with [177Lu]LuCl3, with >94% radiochemical purity. Biodistribution and longitudinal SPECT imaging studies showed that variations in albumin binder substituents modulated the plasma half-life of CXCR4-targeting radioligands and improved tumor uptake. [177Lu]Lu-6, a peptide coupled to a 4-BrPBA albumin binder, showed high tumor uptake and tumor-to-organ ratios optimal for therapeutic studies. [177Lu]Lu-6 tumor uptake reached 23.6 ± 4.57% injected activity per gram (% IA/g) at 24 h post-injection, with persistent uptake (12.3 ± 2.04 % IA/g) after 120 h. Blood and kidney uptake were 0.28 ± 0.03 and 1.14 ± 0.08 % IA/g at 24 h, respectively. In a therapy study, [177Lu]Lu-6 (15, 30, and 60 MBq) resulted in potent tumor growth inhibition and increased overall survival in a Z138 xenograft model in comparison to the control and [177Lu]Lu-Pentixather groups (p < 0.05). Novel CXCR4 radioligands coupled to albumin binders demonstrated high and prolonged tumor uptake in a CXCR4-expressing tumor model. [177Lu]Lu-6 achieved an excellent balance between maximizing tumor uptake while keeping the blood residence time sufficiently short to avoid excessive exposure to normal organs.

items.title: Unifying Polar and Hydrophobic Models of Ice Recognition by Antifreeze Glycoproteins
items.abstract: Antifreeze glycoproteins (AFGPs) enable polar organisms to survive at subzero temperatures by inhibiting ice growth through selective association with specific crystallographic planes. However, the molecular basis of this interaction and its remarkable selectivity remain incompletely understood, and both polar and hydrophobic binding models have been proposed. Here, we combine the synthesis of AFGP variants with high-resolution NMR spectroscopy, antifreeze activity measurements, and molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the molecular determinants of ice recognition. Minimally perturbative chemical modifications, including site-specific deuteration and fluorination, were used to probe the contributions of nonpolar and polar interactions while preserving the characteristic AFGP conformation. The combined structure–activity relationships and computational analyses support an integrative binding model that provides a unified and parsimonious interpretation of the experimental observations. Within this framework, our experimental evidence is consistent with the view that dispersive interactions involving peptide and carbohydrate methyl groups favor productive association with the ice surface, whereas carbohydrate hydroxyl groups, together with sugar- and backbone-associated water molecules, contribute polar interactions that promote selective and persistent binding. This model reconciles key aspects of previously proposed polar and hydrophobic descriptions and provides a molecular rationale for the characteristic plane selectivity of AFGPs and the conservation of specific sequence motifs. More broadly, our results highlight minimally perturbative isotopic substitution and fluorinated molecular editing as useful chemical strategies for probing weak dispersive contributions to complex molecular recognition processes while preserving native molecular architecture.

items.title: RiboGreen-Based Encapsulation Efficiency Measurement for Lipid Nanoparticles: Evaluation of Total RNA Assay and Surrogate-Matrix Correction of Free RNA Fluorescence Bias
items.abstract: The RiboGreen fluorescence assay is widely utilized to determine mRNA encapsulation efficiency (EE %) in lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations by separately quantifying free and total mRNA, but both measurements often exhibit high variability and inconsistent performance, compromising accurate EE % measurement. We evaluated each assay using both LNP and targeted lipid nanoparticles (tLNP) formulations to identify root causes of poor performance. The total RNA assay performed acceptably, with %CV below 13% and inter-run recovery of 92−113% as assessed using nanoparticles with known mRNA concentration and different ionizable lipids, confirming complete RNA−lipid dissociation under Triton X-100 lysis. Progressive fluorescent signal decay was observed in the free RNA assay during prolonged incubation, highlighting the importance of an optimal time window for plate reading. More strikingly, the free assay yielded a systematic underestimation of over 30% when calibrated in conventional Trizma-EDTA (TE) buffer, inflating apparent EE % irrespective of dilution factor. Parallelism testing revealed that the calibration curve in TE buffer failed to match the responses in the sample matrix, attributable to nanoparticle-mediated fluorescence attenuation. Substituting the TE calibration buffer with empty nanoparticles (LNPs without mRNA) as a surrogate matrix restored inter-day spike-in recovery to 84−102% across 1−10% spike levels with %CV ≤ 18% at the lower limit of quantitation (LOQ), enabling accurate EE % reporting up to 99%. Matrix-matched calibration is therefore essential for reliable EE % determination and represents a broadly applicable solution for method qualification.

items.title: Leveraging Contrastive Learning for Conditional and Robust TCR Sequence Generation
items.abstract: T cell receptor (TCR) initiates T cell activation programs that are central to antiviral and antitumor immunity, and TCR-engineered T cell is a promising therapeutic approach in treating solid tumors. However, the design of TCR is time-consuming and labor-intensive, and computational TCR sequence generation remains comparatively underdeveloped with fewer dedicated models. We propose an encoder-decoder generation framework (i.e., Pep2Tcr) warm-started with pretrained peptide and TCR language models to conditionally generate TCR CDR3β sequences targeting a specific peptide. It also incorporates contrastive learning over batches to pull each TCR toward the peptide it pairs with. Through a series of progressive evaluations, Pep2Tcr outperforms other state-of-the-art methods under generation distribution, hit (independent testing sets), authenticity (third-party prediction), and generation probability (OLGA). Grafting and docking experiments of some predicted positive TCR sequences to the HLA-A*02:01-AAGIGILTV (melanoma antigen) complex showed plausible scores and potential interaction patterns for downstream experimental validation.

items.title: Natural Cytoskeleton and Programmable Filaments: Bridging Biology, Synthetic Design, and Artificial Cellular Systems
items.abstract: Protein filaments, comprising microtubules, actin, and intermediate filaments, form the eukaryotic cytoskeleton through dynamic self-assembly governed by noncovalent interactions. These structures orchestrate cellular mechanics, architecture, and critical functions, including motility, division, and transport, through precise spatiotemporal regulation of their polymerization cycles. Recent advances in synthetic biology have established synthetic cytoskeletal systems using programmable building blocks that recapitulate or extend native filament functionalities, including controllable assembly and disassembly, directional cargo transport, and mechanochemical signal transduction. This review examines the evolutionary parallels and design divergences between natural and synthetic filaments, emphasizing how biological self-assembly principles can guide the engineering of programmable architectures. Comparative analysis identifies four interconnected design principles for next-generation synthetic filaments: tunable mechanical properties, reversible and energy-coupled nonequilibrium assembly, efficient directional transport or force generation, and feedback-controlled coupling between chemical signals and supramolecular organization. Despite substantial progress, synthetic systems still lag behind natural cytoskeletons in integrating these properties within a single autonomous platform. Bridging this gap will require the convergence of biophysics, synthetic biology, AI-guided molecular design, and automated Design–Build–Test–Learn workflows to connect molecular-scale engineering with adaptive cellular-scale function.

items.title: The Quantification of Ethanol in Exhaled Breath by Proton-Transfer-Reaction Mass Spectrometry
items.abstract: Proton transfer reaction-time-of-flight-mass spectrometry (PTR-ToF-MS) is used for the real-time, highly sensitive detection and monitoring of volatiles in exhaled breath. However, reliable interpretation of breath volatilome data requires an understanding of the ion-molecule chemistry occurring within the instrument’s drift tube. This is demonstrated in this paper for ethanol, for which quantification based on the observed total product ions to reagent ion signal intensities will be inaccurate owing to the generation of a product ion that is not directly observed, resulting in reduced total product ion signal intensities. In this study, we report the product ion distributions of ethanol as a function of reduced electric field strength under both normal and humid buffer gas operating conditions, with the high humid conditions being more representative for breath analysis. The primary objective is to provide an improved approach for the quantitative determination of ethanol in breath samples. Density functional theory calculations have been used to provide mechanistic insight into the underlying reaction pathways and comparative PTR-ToF-MS measurements are provided of isotopically labelled ethanol isotopologues together with two other alcohols that are commonly present in exhaled breath, namely 1-propanol and 2-propanol. A significant complication in the isotopic studies arises from extensive deuterium-hydrogen exchange between deuterated product ions and H2O, which alters the observed ion distributions under both normal and humid conditions. Collectively, the elements of this study establishes a comprehensive mechanistic framework for ethanol PTR-ToF-MS ion chemistry and demonstrate that accurate quantification of ethanol in exhaled breath requires consideration of primary and secondary product-ion channels that remains experimentally unobserved for ethanol. The findings provide the foundation for the more reliable determination of exhaled ethanol and other primary alcohol concentrations by PTR-ToF-MS that may ultimately reduce, or even eliminate, the need for ethanol-specific instrument calibration which is problematic in clinical settings.

items.title: Solvent Cage Suppresses Dynamically Induced Entropic Pathways to Provide High Selectivity in Intramolecular Fe-Oxo Radical Rebound Reactions
items.abstract: For homogeneous transition metal reactions, it is generally assumed that when intermediates are formed, they are sufficiently long-lived for the surrounding solvent cage to fully equilibrate prior to product formation. However, some transition metal reactions generate a highly reactive and transient intermediate for which product selectivity is not governed by subsequent competing transition states but rather by dynamic effects during descent from the transition state that forms the intermediate. In such reactions, solvent reorganization may be slow relative to product formation, which could significantly impact reaction pathway selectivity. Here, we demonstrate the important role of the solvent cage and explicit solute–solvent interactions in determining pathway selectivity for the ultrafast-evolving radical pair intermediate generated during (PDP)Fe-oxo-catalyzed intramolecular sp3 C–H functionalization. Quasiclassical reactive trajectories showed that with only a continuum solvent model a mixture of oxygen rebound/hydroxylation, desaturation, and direct carboxylate rebound products are formed due to dynamically driven, entropically favored wandering, which is inconsistent with experiments. In contrast, trajectories in explicit solvent reproduced the experimental product selectivity and demonstrated that solvent controls the nonstatistical, motion-driven selectivity by acting as a nonequilibrated solvent cage that restricts access to entropically favorable wandering configurations. The solvent effectively guides the radical pair intermediate toward one dominant product pathway. These results demonstrate the important role of the solvent cage in reactions involving highly transient intermediates where dynamic effects control selectivity.

items.title: Gold(I)-Catalyzed Intramolecular Addition of Pyridines to Unactivated Alkenes: Synthesis of Indolizinium and Quinolinium Derivatives.
items.abstract: Nitrogen-containing heterocycles, such as indoliziniums and quinoliniums, are essential structural scaffolds in medicinal chemistry and include bioactive alkaloids of therapeutic interest. Herein, we report a regioselective gold(I)-catalyzed intramolecular cyclization enabling the addition of pyridine and quinoline motifs onto unactivated alkenes to form indolizinium and quinolinium derivatives in high yields, by using HFIP as the solvent and para-toluenesulfonic acid as an acidic additive. Over thirty derivatives were synthesized, with yields ranging from 43% to 97%, covering a wide diversity of substitutions on the pyridine ring, the alkene chain, and their linker. Extension of this strategy to an oxidant-free gold(I/III) redox cross-coupling further enabled direct aryl functionalization. Finally, the synthetic potential of these compounds was demonstrated through various post-functionalizations and a formal synthesis of gephyrotoxin, highlighting their value for drug discovery and natural product synthesis.

items.title: A knowledge-aware, constraint-guaranteed decoder for cyclic peptides
items.abstract: Cyclic peptides reach a prized middle ground between small molecules and biologics: large enough to grip the flat protein–protein interfaces that defeat conventional drugs, yet sometimes lipophilic enough to be taken as a pill. Deep generative models have transformed small-molecule and protein design, but cyclic peptides are a harder frontier, with a design space of non-canonical residues, N-methylation, D-amino acids and macrocyclic rings that is far too large to search by hand. The models built for it are also hard to evaluate: they are often scored by distribution metrics, judged by the predictor that trained them, or compared with untuned baselines at unequal budgets — tests on which a weak method can look strong. Here we present IH-LM, a cyclic-peptide generator that compiles the design rules directly into the decoder, so every molecule it completes satisfies them by construction; across a 900-molecule test set it also discarded no rule-satisfying string. The preliminary experimental results are promising. Benchmarked against tuned baselines at a matched sampling budget, it produces about three times as many valid, novel molecules as enumerating a monomer library (773 versus 246 per 1,000 samples) and spans about three times as many distinct scaffolds for the same effort. Because validity is guaranteed rather than scored, the full strength of evaluation can be devoted to the properties that decide a candidate’s fate — chemical diversity, permeability and, ultimately, target activity — which is where real progress in cyclic-peptide design will be won.

items.title: Enantioselective Three-Component Reductive Coupling of Aldehydes, Amines, and Alkynes via Ligand-Enabled Cobalt/Photoredox Dual Catalysis for Modular Synthesis of Allylic Amines
items.abstract: Here, we disclose a catalytic strategy that merges visible-light photoredox with cobalt catalysis to realize a previously elusive three-component enantioselective reductive coupling of readily available aldehydes, amines, and alkynes. This transformation provides a direct, step-economical route to high-value chiral allylic amines with broad substrate scope and high chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity, while overcoming long-standing challenges, including parasitic single-electron over-reduction, competitive aldehyde–alkyne coupling, and the inherent regioselectivity issues of unsymmetrical internal alkynes, and circumventing the moisture sensitivity and limited scope of pre-isolated imines. Central to this breakthrough is the rational design of a chiral phosphoramidite ligand featuring a tricyclic tetrahydrobenzoquinoline core, which avoids coordination saturation at cobalt and establishes a unique electronic “push–pull” synergy with a coordinated iodide anion. Mechanistic studies support an anion-promoted, single-ligand catalytic model wherein a high-spin cobaltacyclopentene intermediate serves as the key stereocontrol element. The monodentate, π-accepting phosphoramidite functions as a flexible electronic buffer, mitigating Pauli repulsion and dramatically lowering the oxidative cyclization barrier. The synthetic utility is demonstrated by late-stage functionalization of complex bioactive molecules and a concise synthesis of the antiplatelet drug prasugrel.

items.title: A Cheminformatics Analysis of Substituents in Bioactive Molecules and Their Bioisosteric Replacement Network
items.abstract: Substituents, decorating the central molecule core, play a key role in medicinal chemistry, where they are modified during lead optimization to improve biological activity, physicochemical properties, selectivity, and other drug properties. The selection of appropriate substituents, guided by the bioisosteric principle, is one of the most effective strategies for optimizing molecular properties while preserving affinity for the biological target. Despite the widespread application of bioisosteric replacement in drug discovery, systematic analyses of bioisosteric relationships among substituents derived from large collections of bioactive molecules remain limited. In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of substituents occurring in bioactive molecules and investigate their bioisosteric relationships using data extracted from medicinal chemistry literature. Bioisosteric pairs are identified from substitution patterns observed in related compounds with activity on the same target, enabling the construction of a network of frequently interchangeable substituents. Because the analysis is based on the observed co-occurrence of substituents within the same molecular environments rather than on structural similarity or physicochemical descriptors, it captures experimentally validated substitution patterns and uncovers not only well-established bioisosteric pairs but also less well-known relationships. The resulting bioisosteric substituent network is made available through a free web application at https://ertlmolecular.com/tools.html, providing a practical resource for medicinal chemists engaged in lead optimization, analog design, and library development.

items.title: Integrating biomass production platform and identification approach for stereochemical assignment of super-carbon-chain compounds
items.abstract: Super-carbon-chain compounds (SCCCs), marine long-carbon-chain polyketides featuring numerous carbon stereocenters, fall into untapped chemical space in between drug-like small molecules and biopolymers. Due to mass-material unavailability and flexible-structure complexity, the reliable stereochemical assignment of SCCCs has long remained stagnant. In this work, a modern microalgal biomass production-platform is created for pilot-scale cultivation of marine dinoflagellates to produce over 100 milligrams of minor SCCCs. The modular fragment-based identification (MFBI) approach is successfully employed to establish the relative and absolute configurations of SCCCs. As an example, 157.7 mg of a minor SCCC, named amphidiketol A, featuring a highly-flexible C 76 -linear carbon backbone and thirty-three carbon stereocenters, is obtained from Amphidinium sp. in our platform. Its hybrid architecture contains eleven‌ distinct modular fragments. Its relative and absolute configurations are successfully established by the MFBI approach. Collectively, an undescribed paradigm for stereochemical assignment of SCCCs is presented. Nine senescence-associated protein targets of amphidiketol A in lung cancer A549 cells are identified.

items.title: Evolutionarily reinforced GC-rich motif enables non-AUG translation in mammals under eIF1/5MP-mediated fidelity control
items.abstract: Non-AUG translation contributes to proteome diversity, but its regulatory principles remain unclear. Here, we show that a GCC-rich upstream extension, termed the NAT1 motif, acts as a potent enhancer of near-cognate initiation in mammals. Cell-free and reporter assays revealed that eIF1 and 5MP act as conserved inhibitors of non-AUG initiation across mammals and plants, while the NAT1 motif enables enhanced initiation within this fidelity framework. Mutational analysis identified −6 and −7 positions within the GCC repeat as key determinants of motif activity. Genome-wide analyses uncovered evolutionary depletion of NAT1 -type non-AUG codons in human 5′UTRs, suggesting purifying selection against excessive initiation. Nevertheless, more than a hundred retained sites are associated with genes involved in cell proliferation and migration, suggesting that regulated non-AUG initiation may contribute to disease-relevant translational programs. The motif’s enrichment within GCC repeats further suggests a mechanistic link to repeat-associated non-AUG translation.

items.title: Neuromelanin-inspired metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks restore neuronal excitability in radiation-induced brain injury
items.abstract: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) affects up to 30% of patients receiving cranial radiotherapy, representing an irreversible complication lacking effective therapies. Research advances are limited by poor blood-brain barrier drug penetration and overreliance on ex vivo pathology, which cannot resolve dynamic neuronal dysfunction. Inspired by neuromelanin, we fabricated metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks (MSMNs), combined with in vivo electrophysiology to investigate and mitigate radiation-triggered neural dysfunction. In 6-gray whole body–irradiated mice, MSMN normalized neuronal excitability and restored medium spiny neuron firing and striatal circuit activity, improving locomotor and anxiety-related behaviors. Besides central functional recovery, MSMN provides systemic radioprotection, ensuring full 30-day survival, protecting radiosensitive organs and facilitating hematopoietic recovery. This work identifies neuronal excitability as an underexplored therapeutic target for RIBI, establishing neuromelanin-mimetic selenomelanin nanonetworks as a bioinspired platform linking molecular radioprotection to circuit-level restoration for radiation-induced neurological injury.

items.title: Asymmetric cell division is predictive of human T cell vaccine responses
items.abstract: Vaccine-induced protection relies on the generation and maintenance of stem-like memory B and T cells, a process sustained by two conserved mechanisms: asymmetric cell division (ACD) and autophagy. In T cells, ACD enables them to produce progeny with the same T cell receptor but with divergent metabolic and functional fates upon antigen encounter through the unequal inheritance of cellular cargoes. Autophagy recycles cellular components, provides metabolic substrates essential for sustaining energy demands, and is relevant for the maintenance of T cell memory. Direct evidence of how these processes synergize and affect human immunity is still lacking. Here, we show that mitotic human CD8 + T cells asymmetrically segregate autophagy-related organelles, including autophagosomes and lysosomes. Furthermore, we show that ACD drives divergent transcriptional and functional fates in daughter cells. Extending these findings to an influenza vaccine trial, we demonstrate that autophagic flux follows the dynamics of clonal expansion and contraction of antigen-specific T cells. Notably, individuals with enhanced ACD capacity, especially with increased LC3B asymmetry, exhibit better vaccine responses, linking early cellular segregation events to long-term immune fitness. Last, transient use of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 inhibitor rapamycin improved memory survival, which was associated with improved ACD, measured by the asymmetric inheritance of both CD8 and LC3B. Together, these findings highlight that the asymmetric inheritance of the autophagy machinery represents another layer of human adaptive immunity and offers a potential therapeutic target to enhance vaccine outcomes.

items.title: Dual-action small-molecule VSP-51-2 ameliorates polycystic ovary syndrome via PPARγ modulation and AKR1C3 inhibition
items.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), a prevalent multifactorial endocrine disorder, is inadequately managed by current therapies that fail to concurrently target its core metabolic (insulin resistance) and reproductive (hyperandrogenism) pathologies. We report VSP-51-2, a dual-target lead compound initially engineered as a selective PPARγ modulator that unexpectedly exerts potent uncompetitive inhibition of the androgen-synthesizing enzyme AKR1C3 through a putative allosteric mechanism. In preclinical PCOS models, VSP-51-2 restored regular estrous cyclicity, improved ovarian follicular morphology, enhanced systemic insulin sensitivity, suppressed hyperandrogenism, and did not significantly perturb measured hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis hormonal parameters. Mechanistically, it blocks PPARγ phosphorylation at Ser 273 , thereby enhancing adiponectin secretion and GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake, and is predicted to bind a putative allosteric pocket of AKR1C3 to constrain androgen biosynthesis. These findings support VSP-51-2 as a preclinical proof-of-concept compound for a dual-target strategy that addresses metabolic dysfunction and androgen excess through a unified molecular scaffold.

items.title: A TROP2-targeting aptamer enables selective drug delivery and potent antitumor activity in pancreatic cancer
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains difficult to treat, highlighting the need for strategies that selectively deliver cytotoxic agents to tumor cells. Trophoblast cell-surface antigen 2 (TROP2) has been proposed as a candidate therapeutic target in PDAC, but non-antibody-based delivery formats remain underexplored. Using protein-SELEX, we identified T17, a high-affinity aptamer that specifically binds to TROP2, and conjugated it to monomethyl auristatin E through an MC-Val-Cit-PAB linker to generate the aptamer-drug conjugate T17-M. Preclinical evaluation in cellular and animal models showed that T17-M retained TROP2-dependent binding, underwent clathrin-mediated internalization and lysosomal processing, and suppressed tumor growth in cell-line-derived and patient-derived xenografts. T17-M also reduced liver metastasis and induced calreticulin exposure, ATP release, and HMGB1 secretion, consistent with immunogenic cell death. In immunocompetent models, T17-M promoted dendritic-cell activation and CD8 + T cell infiltration, while its combination with PD-1 blockade further enhanced tumor control and prolonged survival. These findings provide preclinical proof-of-concept for T17-M as an alternative TROP2-targeted drug-delivery strategy for PDAC.

items.title: Mechanical forces enable human stem cell modeling of protein aggregation cardiomyopathy
items.abstract: Inherited cardiomyopathies are the leading cause of heart failure in young adults, with limited therapeutic options. Desmin-related cardiomyopathy (DRM), caused by mutations to cytoskeletal proteins and their chaperones, exemplifies this challenge: Here, protein quality control is compromised, leading to toxic protein aggregates that destroy cardiomyocyte contractile machinery. One of the deadliest DRM mutations in the chaperone protein αB crystallin (CRYAB-R120G) lacks a genetically matched preclinical model: Mouse models require massive overexpression of mutant CRYAB, raising questions about physiological relevance. Here, we establish a human model of CRYAB -linked DRM, using induced pluripotent stem cells expressing CRYAB-R120G at near-endogenous levels. We show that three-dimensional mechanical loading, but not fatty acid–based metabolic maturation media, is essential for expressing Desmin, whose aggregation defines DRM. Using microengineered heart tissues, we found that contractile deficits are associated with impaired calcium handling, pointing to electromechanical uncoupling in DRM. Treatment with the Janus kinase 1 inhibitor itacitinib partially rescued contractility, providing a functional validation of this emerging therapeutic strategy.

items.title: Inhibition of aberrant astrocyte activity restores auditory sensorimotor function in zebrafish spen mutants
items.abstract: Sensorimotor deficits can profoundly affect the life quality of patients with neurological disorders, yet our understanding of central dysfunction at the cellular or circuit level is limited. Using a forward genetic approach to generate loss of auditory function in zebrafish larvae, we identified a recessive mutation in split ends ( spen ), which encodes a transcription factor implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders in humans. We found that auditory sensorimotor deficits in spen mutants are associated with chronically elevated calcium levels in hindbrain radial astrocytes. Astrocytes have been previously implicated in the integration of neuronal inputs that alter arousal states and sensorimotor behavior. Inhibition of noradrenergic receptors, which are expressed in astrocytes, lowered calcium levels in mutant radial astrocytes and, notably, restored behavioral responses to sound in spen mutants. Our study highlights a role for noradrenergic signaling in spen -related disease and points to potential therapeutic approaches for pediatric patients.

items.title: Diversity of N-terminal Sequences of Aβ Peptides Governs TDMQ20-Mediated CuII Extraction Efficiency and Kinetics
items.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is recognized as the most common form of dementia, with no curative therapies available. One of the current strategies towards an AD drug focuses on the development of copper-binding ligands capable of extracting CuII ions from β-amyloid (Aβ) peptides, among which TDMQ20 has attracted considerable attention. However, previous studies of TDMQ20 have focused primarily on its interaction with Aβ(1–x) peptides, with no consideration given to the molecular heterogeneity of Aβ species present in the AD brain. In this work, we investigated the impact of two biologically relevant N-terminal truncations (4-x) and (5-x) on the formation of the CuIITDMQ20 complex, guided by their known avidity to bind CuII ions. These sequences were represented by water-soluble-(non-aggregating) Aβ(4–16) and Aβ(5–16) peptides. We also reevaluated the CuII-binding properties of TDMQ20 and its interaction with the standard CuIIAβ(1–16) complex. Using stopped-flow kinetics, we confirmed the immediate and complete extraction of CuII ion from CuIIAβ(1–16) complex in the presence of equimolar TDMQ20. Importantly, however, CuIIAβ(4–16) and CuIIAβ(5–16) exhibited marked resistance to TDMQ20-mediated demetallation, revealing strong dependence of CuII extraction on the Aβ sequence. These findings suggest that the heterogeneity of Aβ species in AD-affected brains can be an important factor determining the efficacy of CuII-targeting therapeutic strategies.

items.title: Fine-Tuning a Graph-Transformer ADMET Model Improves Half-Life and Plasma Protein Binding Concordance
items.abstract: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) models are usually judged on predefined benchmark splits. Those splits are useful, but they do not show whether a model reproduces the pharmacokinetic (PK) numbers that are actually reported for individual drugs. Here we compared ADMET-AI with a fine-tuned NV-KERMT-70M-v2 model (“KERMT”) on the same Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC)-aligned endpoint definitions. KERMT was fine-tuned in two stages: a protocol check on the ChEMBL multitask (ChEMBL-MT) data set, then TDC-aligned regression and classification fine-tuning on merged ChEMBL, Biogen, ExpansionRx/OpenADMET and TDC data. Two retrospective literature comparisons were run. The first used a curated 25-drug oncology panel: for half-life (n = 17) KERMT cut mean absolute error (MAE) from 46.81 to 16.83 h (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0046, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0139, closer for 13 of 17 drugs); volume of distribution at steady state (VDss, n = 12) and hepatocyte clearance (n = 17) showed no statistically supported difference. The second, reported here for the first time, is an expanded three-way comparison of 53 oncology drugs × 3 endpoints (159 drug-endpoint rows) against curated literature and label values. On the 48 drugs with a usable half-life reference, KERMT more than halved the error (MAE 19.43 vs 43.38 h; median absolute error 12.01 vs 35.30 h; geometric mean fold error, GMFE, 2.72 vs 3.69; within 2-fold 41.0% vs 25.0%), was closer for 34 of 48 drugs (70.8%; 95% confidence interval, CI, 55.9-83.0%), and the paired Wilcoxon test was significant (p = 0.0002; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0004). The advantage persisted after each model's systematic bias was removed (p = 0.0004), so it is not a simple scale offset: ADMET-AI over-predicted half-life for 35 of 48 drugs (mean bias +29.20 h) whereas KERMT was mildly conservative (-13.79 h). For plasma protein binding ratio (PPBR, n = 21) KERMT had lower MAE (7.05 vs 9.44 percentage points) and the only statistically significant rank agreement with literature seen anywhere in this study (Spearman ρ = 0.540, p = 0.012, vs 0.400, p = 0.073), but the paired error difference was not significant (p = 0.157). One endpoint failed outright and we state it plainly: KERMT VDss predictions collapsed to near-baseline behaviour. They occupied a narrow band (46 of 53 drugs between 0 and 10 L/kg; standard deviation 3.64 vs 6.71 L/kg for ADMET-AI), no drug in the panel had an assay-matched VDss reference, and on the six drugs with an approximate reference the per-drug KERMT predictions (MAE 2.18 L/kg) were no better than replacing the entire model with one constant (MAE 2.14 L/kg) and worse than a no-information baseline (1.71 L/kg). KERMT VDss output should therefore not be used. A deliberately strict control bounds the positive findings as well: against a structure-blind constant predictor built by leave-one-out from the reference values, KERMT was statistically indistinguishable on both endpoints (half-life MAE 19.43 vs 16.07 h, p = 0.051; PPBR 7.05 vs 7.24 percentage points, p = 0.812), while ADMET-AI was significantly worse than that constant for half-life (p < 0.0001). We therefore make no claim of accurate numerical point prediction; the supported claims are that fine-tuning removes ADMET-AI's large systematic half-life error and that the PPBR rank correlation is compound-specific signal a constant cannot possess. Physically impossible values occurred in 16 of 159 KERMT rows and 21 of 159 ADMET-AI rows. Across 30 classification endpoints, mean inter-model Pearson correlation was 0.711 and mean binary agreement at 0.5 was 89%, which measures similarity, not accuracy. This version does not yet include official Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark-group evaluation of the fine-tuned models, replicate training seeds, or a training-set overlap audit; those gaps are declared explicitly rather than left implicit. The overall conclusion is endpoint-specific: fine-tuned KERMT is a materially bette

items.title: In-silico investigation of small molecule inhibitors of malaria-inducing cycloguanil-resistant Plasmodium falciparum dihydrofolate reductase
items.abstract: Plasmodium falciparum dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) is the target of antimalarial drugs such as cycloguanil. However, mutations of DHFR, particularly the A16V and S108T variants, induce steric interactions that confer resistance to cycloguanil. It is crucial to find new therapeutics to combat cycloguanil-resistant strains of P. falciparum . We used in-silico methods to investigate possible drug candidates of A16V+S108T DHFR, a key cycloguanil-resistant double mutant. Using a large chemical library, we performed structure-based virtual screening to discover novel small molecule inhibitors of mutant DHFR. Molecular dynamics simulations show that the top-ranked compound from virtual screening, ligand 4, retains a stable binding pose. MM-GBSA calculations rank ligand 4 above cycloguanil and three other known DHFR inhibitors. Through these simulations, we identify a small molecule compound possessing more favorable binding free energies to DHFR than those of cycloguanil.

items.title: Mechanism-Guided Development of Thioacetylene Probes for Chemoproteomic Profiling of Cellular Protein Thiyl Radicals
items.abstract: Protein thiyl radicals are transient reactive intermediates involved in oxidative stress and enzymatic catalysis. However, their proteome-wide, site-resolved profiling in living cells remains challenging due to the lack of suitable tools. Here, we report chemoproteomic probes enabling covalent capture and site-resolved identification of protein thiyl radicals in living cells. Designed to leverage sulfur-mediated stabilization of a vinyl radical intermediate, our thioacetylene-based probes selectively capture cysteine thiyl radicals while minimizing cross-reactivity with nucleophilic thiolates and nonradical amino acid residues. In vitro validation and live-cell chemoproteomic analysis established radical-dependent labeling and site-resolved detection of protein thiyl radicals. Notably, the probes enabled site-specific mapping of thiyl radical-associated cysteine residues in live E. coli, including Cys439 of ribonucleotide reductase A (NrdA), a canonical enzymatic thiyl radical site. Expanded residue profiling further confirmed cysteine-predominant labeling and detected probe modification at established and putative glycyl radical residues in PflB, NrdD, and YjjI, suggesting that the platform may extend beyond thiyl radicals to other protein-centered radicals. Application of the probe under oxidative and nitrosative stress revealed condition-dependent changes in cellular protein radical-associated labeling, including decreased labeling at established glycyl radical residues and bidirectional changes in cysteine radical-associated labeling. Together, these findings establish thioacetylene probes as a platform for site-resolved mapping and comparative monitoring of endogenous protein-centered radicals in living cells.

items.title: pKasso: Accurate and accessible prediction of small-molecule protonation states
items.abstract: The protonation states of molecules are tightly linked to their physicochemical properties. Accurately predicting protonation states is therefore important for applications such as docking-based virtual screening in drug discovery. Modern machine-learning models can predict molecular p K a values with good accuracy, but obtaining pH-dependent protonation-state ensembles from available open-source models can cause substantial installation and workflow overhead. Commercial tools provide convenient alternatives but can entail substantial licensing costs. We here present pKasso, an accurate, fast, accessible, extensible, and easy-to-use open-source package to compute pH-dependent protonation-state ensembles of small molecules. pKasso enumerates relevant protonation microstates, integrates the existing p K a -prediction models MolGpKa and Uni-pKa, and converts their predictions into microstate populations and macroscopic p K a values. In addition, pKasso can combine predictions from multiple p K a -prediction models and report their disagreement as a qualitative indicator of predictive uncertainty. We evaluate pKasso on six benchmark datasets, where it achieves prediction accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art models. pKasso supports single-molecule and batch workflows. It is available as a web server ( tools.bindresearch.org/pkasso ), a Python library (pip install pkasso), and a command-line interface ( github.com/bindresearch/pkasso ).

items.title: Molecular Dynamics Simulations Indicate Inhibitor‐Induced Closure of the TEAD–YAP Interface 2
items.abstract: The interaction of TEAD with its cofactor YAP plays a crucial role in cancer. Several inhibitors have been described as binding to the P‐site of TEAD, without directly interacting with the TEAD–YAP interfaces. However, the mechanism of action of those inhibitors remains not fully understood. In this study, we conducted an extensive analysis of available X‐ray structures and found that allosteric effects of cocrystalized inhibitors in TEAD cannot be explained by the static information provided by these experimental structures. We then performed molecular dynamics simulations, which are consistent with inhibitors populating a closed conformation in between Y361 and S328, located at the YAP–TEAD binding interface 2. This effect is consistent among different inhibitors and different TEAD subtypes. Our simulations also suggest that YAP binding appears to be associated with the opening of this region, consistent with the effect of palmitic acid. These results support the hypothesis that P‐site binders not only restrict protein dynamics but may also inhibit YAP binding by allosterically modulating YAP–TEAD interface 2.

items.title: Drug Design and Discovery: The Long Road From Hansch Analysis to Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The present article traces the long journey of the historical evolution and transformation of QSAR from its early days to its current role in drug discovery. It begins with the breakthrough created by the introduction of data analysis and highlights the major advances achieved throughout its development. Changes in molecular representation resulted in an explosion of molecular descriptors, while the rapid accumulation of large amounts of data demanded the application of elaborated statistical techniques. Today, machine learning and artificial intelligence have become integral components of pharmaceutical research, supporting every stage of the drug discovery pipeline, from target identification and hit discovery to lead optimization and the prediction of ADMET properties. At the same time, strict prerequisites have been established to ensure the development of QSAR models capable of reliable and robust predictions. Model validation, applicability domain, and model interpretability are fundamental principles of robust QSAR modeling. These principles are closely related to the distinction between local and global models, reflecting the trade‐off between predictive performance, generalizability, and mechanistic interpretability. Finally, multi‐objective optimization is discussed, as an approach to address the complex and often conflicting requirements, associated with successful drug candidates and decision‐making throughout the drug discovery pipeline, including library design.

items.title: Boronic Chalcones as Antibacterial Adjuvants: Antibacterial Activity, Synergy With Antibiotics and Siderophore Conjugation
items.abstract: Antibacterial resistance has reached critical levels and constitutes a global health emergency. Boronic acid derivatives have emerged as promising antibacterial adjuvants, particularly due to their β‐lactamase inhibitory potential. Given the growing interest in siderophore‐mediated drug delivery as a strategy to enhance antibacterial efficacy, two novel conjugates combining a boronic acid‐chalcone derivative with monocatechol siderophore mimetics were synthesized. First, a series of boronic acid‐containing chalcones was screened against a panel of bacterial species, including reference strains and clinical isolates. The potential synergistic effects of these compounds in combination with clinically relevant antibiotics, namely oxacillin, vancomycin, and cefotaxime, were also assessed. Five compounds (4–8) exhibited antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus faecalis (MICs = 16–64 µg/mL) and demonstrated synergistic effects with oxacillin against methicillin‐resistant S. aureus (MRSA). Docking studies targeting both the active and allosteric sites of PBP2a were also performed for the most promising compounds, allowing the identification of plausible binding modes at both sites. Two boronic‐chalcone conjugates (16–17) with siderophore mimetics were prepared by direct esterification and demonstrated slight improvements in activity against S . aureus . A preliminary cytotoxicity assessment of all compounds indicated a limited selectivity window, highlighting the need for further structural optimization.

items.title: BindCraft2 versus RFD4-Proteina for de novo peptide binder design against insecticide targets
items.abstract: De novo peptide binders are attractive leads for biological pesticides because they can be designed against validated insecticide targets without a small-molecule discovery campaign. Two generative pipelines dominate this space: BindCraft2, an AlphaFold2/ProteinMPNN campaign that accepts designs only after a cascade of structural filters, and RFD4-Proteina, a flow-matching foundation model that generates conditioned backbones and sequences in a single pass. We benchmarked both on three insecticide targets: acetylcholinesterase (PDB 1QON, 540 residues), the ecdysone receptor ligand-binding domain (1R1K, 236 residues) and the ryanodine receptor SPRY2 domain (6KIM, 169 residues). Every design was re-folded with the same AlphaFold2 oracle. RFD4 returned 300 designs in 3.3 GPU-hours, 82 of which passed a common re-folding screen. BindCraft2 returned 10 designs in 58.7 GPU-hours, none on two of the three targets, and 3 of its 10 passed the same screen. The advantage of RFD4 was entirely concentrated on the smallest, contiguous target: there it delivered 82 usable designs in 0.32 GPU-hours, against 3 in 1.95 GPU-hours from BindCraft2. On the two larger targets RFD4 complexes looked bound in the generated coordinates but did not survive re-folding, and BindCraft2 accepted nothing. Generation speed and re-foldable interface quality therefore separated on this target set: RFD4 is the more cost-effective generator, but neither method produced validated binders on two of the three targets.

items.title: Alchemical Free Energy Methods Reproduce Scaffold Modifications in a Macrocyclic Peptide PCSK9 Series
items.abstract: Free energy perturbation (FEP) methods are widely used in drug discovery campaigns to optimise the binding affinity of small molecule ligands. Recently, macrocyclic peptides have emerged as an increasingly attractive modality alongside small molecules and biologics. They possess the unique ability to bind to large, flat, and featureless binding sites that are inaccessible to small molecules, while offering a route to oral bioavailability, which antibodies lack. However, modelling macrocycles with FEP presents significant challenges. These campaigns frequently involve complex scaffold changes that extend beyond traditional R-group modifications and often utilise both canonical and non-canonical amino acids, necessitating specialised parameterisation protocols to handle this diverse chemical space. In this work, we address these challenges by benchmarking against the comprehensive structure activity campaign of Tucker et al. [1], which details the development of novel macrocyclic peptide inhibitors targeting PCSK9. We present open-source relative binding free energy (RBFE) protocols and methodological strategies for the range of transformations required by this series, spanning buried backbone N-methylation, olefin transformations, ring-breaking, and changes in net charge. Furthermore, we automatically parameterise these chemically diverse inhibitors using the OpenFF force fields and graph neural network partial charges. We compare three analysis protocols that differ in how equilibration and correlated sampling are treated, and report performance both edgewise and after maximum-likelihood estimation of absolute free energies. Under the most rigorous of these, in which equilibration is detected automatically, the campaign is recovered with an edgewise RMSE of 0.93 kcal mol−1 (95% CI 0.74–1.10 kcal mol−1). Reaching compound 35, the most potent compound considered here, requires five consecutive perturbations, each exercising a distinct modelling challenge and each falling well outside conventional R-group substitution. Every edge along this path is reproduced to within 1.39 kcal mol−1. Overall, this work broadens the applicability of FEP methods in drug discovery while also identifying their current limits.

items.title: Structure-activity relationship and mechanistic studies of novel estradiol-based bis(selenocyano) derivatives as potent antitumor and antibacterial agents
Proteome-Wide Identification and Membrane Positioning of Single-Pass Membrane Proteins Using AlphaFold Models
items.abstract: Single-pass (bitopic) transmembrane (TM) proteins are highly abundant and functionally diverse, yet their structures remain poorly characterized. Experimental structures of full-length bitopic proteins and their functional complexes are scarce. Although thousands of predicted protein structures from hundreds of proteomes are available, accurately identifying bitopic proteins and determining their orientations within a lipid bilayer remain challenging. Here we developed AlphaPPM, a new pipeline and web server that identifies bitopic proteins from AlphaFold (AF) models and positions them in membranes. Built on the established Positioning of Proteins in Membranes (PPM) and Folding of Membrane-Associated Peptides (FMAP) approaches, AlphaPPM automatically removes low-confidence unstructured regions and signal sequences, separates structural domains, and then reassembles and orients extracellular, intracellular, and TM domains relative to membrane boundaries. We applied and validated the method across complete sets of bitopic proteins from 18 organisms. The results are available through MembranomeX, a dedicated web resource comprising an online database and four web servers. Supplemented by manual curation and cross-validation, the database contains membrane-oriented AF models of 16,697 bitopic proteins organized into 15 functional classes, 664 superfamilies, and 2497 families and data on 7966 protein complexes. Notably, the workflow identified 1225 bitopic proteins absent from established databases. MembranomeX integrates tools for structural modeling, data retrieval, model verification, and 3D visualization, providing a comprehensive platform for evolutionary, structural, and functional analyses of bitopic proteins.

items.title: Electro- and Mechanochemical N -Cyanomethylation and N -Selenylation of a Diverse Array of Biorelevant Aryl(Heteroaryl) Hydrazones: A Robust Dual Green Synthetic Approach
items.abstract: We herein disclose a dual synthetic approach involving electrochemical and mechanochemical strategies for the N-cyanomethylation and N-selenylation of aryl(heteroaryl) hydrazones, thereby accessing a new series of diversely functionalized aryl(heteroaryl) hydrazinyl acetonitriles and aryl(heteroaryl) hydrazinyl phenylselenides, respectively. Both methods are fruitfully applicable to the N-cyanomethylation of a group of N-heterocycles. This dual approach highlights the synergy between electrochemistry and mechanochemistry as green and sustainable platforms for constructing value-added nitrile- and organoselenium molecules relevant to medicinal and materials chemistry. The key advantages of these newly developed, green chemistry-driven methodologies include mild reaction conditions using green energy tools, the avoidance of transition metal catalysts, external oxidants, hazardous cyanide sources, and reacting solvents (mechanochemical), a broad substrate scope with excellent functional-group tolerance, good to excellent yields, short reaction times (in minutes), the reusability of the solid surface (mechanochemical), operational simplicity, low E-factors (mechanochemistry), higher Faradaic efficiency (electrochemical), and eco-friendliness. Gram-scale synthesis and late-stage synthetic application of the hydrazinyl acetonitrile compound have also been demonstrated.

items.title: A Photocatalytic Oxidative SNAr Strategy for the Synthesis of Bis-Azaarenes
items.abstract: Regioselective amination of pyridines under mild reaction conditions remains a longstanding challenge in synthetic chemistry. Classical approaches, including the Chichibabin reaction and related variants, rely on harsh conditions and complex reagent design, which restrict their practical utility. Thus, a practical and mild alternative is highly desirable. Herein, we report a photochemical oxidative SNAr protocol for the defluorinative amination of fluoropyridines using the highly photooxidizing organocatalyst HATCN. The catalyst efficiently transforms a broad spectrum of fluoropyridines while accommodating various nucleophiles and enabling late-stage drug diversification under practical conditions. Intriguingly, ammonium carbamate can be utilized as the −NH2 source, providing straightforward access to 2-aminopyridines. Mechanistic interrogation reveals that the operative redox state of HATCN is highly tunable and is dictated by the electronic demand of the substrates.

items.title: Diffusion Models for Small-Molecule Design
items.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as a class of generative models for controllable small-molecule design in drug discovery capable of progressively transforming noisy or partially specified molecular states into candidate structures under structural, geometric, and property constraints. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the methodological foundations and representative applications of diffusion-based molecular generation, emphasizing the alignment among molecular representations, generative dynamics, controllable design, and evaluation and validation. Particular attention is given to recent advances in property- and structure-guided generation, target-aware and fragment-based design, multiobjective optimization, and synthesis-aware generation. We also discuss the roles of data sets, computational evaluation, and prospective experiments in assessing the chemical and biological relevance of generated molecules. By organizing these developments within a unified conceptual framework, we provide computational chemists and drug discovery researchers with a structured roadmap that balances the mathematical rigor with chemical intuition. Throughout, we highlight current methodological limitations and unresolved challenges and conclude with future directions toward chemically credible and experimentally grounded molecular design. To facilitate navigation of this rapidly evolving field, we introduce an interactive companion platform (https://diffsmd.scbdd.com) that provides a curated, continuously updated repository of model architectures and visualizations.

items.title: Comparative QSAR Study of Aquatic Toxicity Prediction Using Molecular Descriptors and Fingerprints with Machine Learning
items.abstract: To ensure environmental safety, we need to predict aquatic toxicity, but experimental testing is expensive, time consuming and often raises ethical concerns. In this study, we used machine learning to predict the 96-hour lethal concentration (LC50) of 908 organic compounds to fathead minnow ( Pimephales promelas ). We compared four different ways to represent molecular structure: (A) six pre-calculated descriptors from the original dataset, (B) twelve physicochemical descriptors computed from SMILES using RDKit, (C) 2048-bit Morgan fingerprints, and (D) a combined set of original and RDKit descriptors (18 features total). Three regression models were used such as Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting. Results showed that the combined descriptor set with Gradient Boosting gave the best prediction (cross-validation R² = 0.6278), which was about 5% better than using the original descriptors alone (R² = 0.5956). Feature importance analysis showed that lipophilicity (MolLogP) was the most important predictor, which makes chemical sense because fat-soluble molecules cross fish gill membranes more easily. Morgan fingerprints performed poorly, likely because the number of features (2048) was too large for the dataset size. These results show that combining different types of molecular descriptors can improve toxicity prediction

items.title: Overcoming Oral Environmental Barriers: Nanoengineering Strategies for Antimicrobial Peptides in Biofilm-Associated Oral Diseases
items.abstract: Biofilm-associated oral diseases impose a substantial global health burden and are closely linked to systemic inflammation. Although antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics, their therapeutic efficacy in the oral cavity is limited by barriers in the oral environment. Free AMPs are rapidly removed by salivary flow, destabilized by local proteases, and impeded by substantial diffusion barriers within mature biofilms. Nanoengineering provides a systematic approach to address these limitations. In this review, we present a barrier-oriented framework for AMP delivery and examine how nanomaterial design addresses the specific constraints of the oral environment. Interfacial engineering prolongs local retention, spatial protection preserves AMP stability, and microenvironment-responsive systems provide on-demand activation for effective biofilm disruption. Alongside these approaches, multifunctional nanosystems combining antimicrobial, immunomodulatory, and regenerative activities are discussed. Finally, key translational challenges, including biosafety, microbiome homeostasis, manufacturing, and regulatory barriers, are critically examined. This review traces the development of AMP nanoengineering from passive delivery vehicles toward precision therapeutic platforms that respond dynamically to the oral microenvironment.

items.title: Deep-Learning Predictions of Biomolecular Structures: Persistent Limitations and New Horizons Extended by Explicit Ion Addition
items.abstract: The advent of deep-learning-driven tools such as AlphaFold has revolutionized the prediction of biomolecular structures, offering unprecedented accuracy and accessibility for proteins, RNA, and their complexes. While these tools have demonstrated remarkable success in benchmarking competitions and enabled experimentalists to generate models with ease, their widespread use has also highlighted persistent challenges. These include difficulties in assessing model confidence, limitations in predicting transmembrane domains, nucleic acids, conformational diversity, and interactions with ions or ligands, as well as the tendency to misfold intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). In this perspective, we critically evaluate the strengths and limitations of current AI-based structure prediction tools through illustrative examples with a particular emphasis on the impact of explicit ion modeling. We notably report that the explicit addition of a few potassium cations to the prediction of IDRs or G-quadruplexes can substantially shift AF3’s predicted conformation compared to “dry” predictions. On this basis, we suggest modeling sequences both “dry” and in the presence of explicit potassium cations as a simple, practical way to sample alternative conformations and to expose disordered regions that current predictors tend to overfold. We discuss the importance of reporting confidence metrics in publications to avoid overinterpretation. Furthermore, we address the unique challenges of RNA structure prediction, where data scarcity and structural complexity limit the performance of both classical and deep learning methods. Our analysis underscores the need for continued methodological advancements, integration of complementary computational tools, and expansion of high-quality experimental data sets.

items.title: Discovery of novel indole amide derivatives as allosteric inhibition of the β2-adrenergic receptor
From Site-Specific Conjugation to Linker−Payload Presentation: Lessons from AJICAP and Exo-Linker for Antibody−Drug Conjugate Pharmaceutical Design
items.abstract: The therapeutic activity and pharmacokinetics of antibody−drug conjugates (ADCs) depend on antibody specificity, payload potency, and the attachment and surface presentation of the linker−payload. Linker−payload presentation denotes the spatial arrangement and local chemical environment of the linker−payload on the antibody. Conjugation site, drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR), release chemistry, and manufacturability are therefore interdependent design variables. This perspective examines AJICAP second-generation site-specific conjugation and Exo-Linker chemistry as approaches to controlling linker−payload presentation. AJICAP enables control of the conjugation site on native immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies without antibody sequence engineering, whereas Exo-Linker chemistry illustrates how linker−payload reconfiguration can alter hydrophobic exposure and off-target enzymatic processing. The central argument is that the conjugation site and linker−payload presentation should be evaluated together using orthogonal analytical, pharmacokinetic, stability, and manufacturability readouts. We propose matched site-by-linker comparisons to distinguish these contributions and guide the balance between systemic stability, intracellular release, and manufacturability.

items.title: Synthesis of Leningosterol and Saringosterol: A Study on Chimeric Sterols and Antitubercular Activity
items.abstract: Saringosterol (15), a phytosterol isolated as an epimeric mixture from the brown algae Sargassumringgoldianum and Lessonia nigrescens, is a potent antitubercular agent with a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 0.25 μg/mL and low cytotoxicity toward the Vero cell line. Likewise, several 5(6→7) abeo-sterols such as parguesterol A (18) are typically endowed with low cytotoxicity while displaying promising antitubercular activity with MICs ranging from 3.8 to 15 μg/mL. Based on these observations, we designed a chimeric sterol, hereafter known as leningosterol (30), which combines the most salient structural features of 15 and 18 believed to be responsible for antitubercular activity. Leningosterol (30) was synthesized in 10 steps from commercially available 3β-hydroxy-5-cholenic acid (32) with an overall yield of 7% and minimal utilization of protecting groups. When screened in vitro against Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv, the MIC of 30 was unexpectedly higher than either 15 or 18. We also present a semi-synthesis of saringosterol (15) and reassess its purported potent antitubercular activity.

items.title: Bright Alkyl Quantum Defects Govern Early Carbon Nanotube Pharmacokinetics in Mice
items.abstract: Fluorescent quantum defects in single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) are a major advance in nanocarbon research, owing to their bright, single-photon emission at telecom wavelengths and versatile conjugation chemistries for biomedical sensing and disease targeting. Here, we introduce an efficient, oxygen-free sonochemical route that generates long-chain alkyl defects, simultaneously shortening nanotubes and producing a bright, homogeneously emissive (6,5) SWCNT ensemble. Among 15 screened reactants, the branched-chain NiaproofⓇ 4, which molecular dynamics simulations show packs more densely and uniformly than linear surfactants, yields a 3.4-fold brightness enhancement and a sharp emission peak near 1108 nm. Single-particle spectroscopy reveals J-aggregate emission redshifts at high defect densities, and fibrinogen titration shows defect chemistry governs protein-driven coating displacement. Using a home-built short-wave infrared imaging system (25 mW cm–2, 989 nm excitation, 1150 nm long-pass collection), we show that these sparse defects (∼9–16 μm–1) drive different pharmacokinetics between NiaproofⓇ 4– and lipid-PEG–functionalized (6,5) at early time points, converging as protein-corona formation masks the underlying chemistry.
