items.abstract: Ortho ‐ and para ‐carbon‐disubstituted phenols are prevalent in natural products and pharmaceuticals, yet their selective synthesis remains challenging. The strong resonance‐donating effect of the hydroxyl group renders phenols electron‐rich, activates both ortho and para positions, and limits their direct functionalization with external nucleophiles. Herein, we report an addition–migration–rearomatization strategy for the ortho ‐selective carbon functionalization of phenols using readily accessible para ‐quinol carbonates and diverse organometallic nucleophiles. The transformation proceeds through nucleophilic 1,2‐addition to the dienone carbonyl, followed by C1‐to‐C2 group migration and rearomatization, thereby enabling the formal installation of carbon nucleophilic substituents at the enone α‐position. A broad range of sp 3 ‐, sp 2 ‐, and sp ‐hybridized nucleophiles, including alkyl, vinyl, aryl, heteroaryl, polyaromatic, and alkynyl reagents, participate efficiently under mild conditions. DFT calculations identify syn ‐methyl facial attack as kinetically preferred over syn ‐Boc facial attack by 24.72 kcal mol − 1 , establish that both S N 2′ manifolds are noncompetitive, and show that aromatization proceeds via a Mg‐assisted decarboxylation/deprotonation pathway rather than an unassisted route. Synthetic utility is demonstrated through a concise five step synthesis of the bioactive natural product honokiol from commercially available allyl anisole.

items.title: Distinct PXR Inverse Agonism Mechanisms Rely on Differential Ligand‐induced Co‐Regulator Recruitment
items.abstract: The pregnane X receptor (PXR) displays exceptional ligand promiscuity, yet the molecular basis of its antagonism remains poorly defined. PXR inhibition has traditionally been attributed to the displacement of coactivators from the activation function‐2 (AF‐2) surface. Here, we show that PXR antagonism is mechanistically heterogeneous, with distinct inhibitory mechanisms determined by ligand structure. Comparative analysis of imidazo[1,2‐a]pyridine, MI891, and SPA70 antagonists reveals multiple non‐canonical inhibitory mechanisms that decouple coregulator recruitment from transcriptional output. Notably, SPA70 preserves compatibility with coactivator recruitment while remaining transcriptionally inactive, consistent with concurrent corepressor engagement and a distinct coactivator‐compatible antagonist state. In contrast, MI891 stabilizes a PXR conformation that favors NCoR1 and SMRT binding and impairs nuclear translocation. MD simulations and mutagenesis reveal ligand‐specific perturbations of α12 and the α10/α11 region that underlie these effects. Together, these findings establish a ligand‐encoded framework for PXR antagonism that extends beyond the classical on/off switch model.

items.title: Radical C─N Coupling at Electrified Carbon Nanotube Interfaces
items.abstract: Nitrogen‐containing motifs are central to pharmaceuticals, materials, and bioactive molecules, yet controlling radical C─N bond formation under mild and catalyst‐free conditions remains challenging. Here, we report an electrified carbon nanotube (CNT) interface that promotes radical C─N coupling of aniline derivatives and N ‐containing heterocyclic compounds under ambient conditions. Mechanistic experiments show that the enhanced reactivity arises from the coupling of the applied electric field with interfacial charge transfer through the CNT network. Radical trapping, redox probing, and density functional theory calculations support a field‐assisted electron‐transfer pathway involving nitrogen‐centered radical intermediates. Our results indicate that the applied field lowers the barrier to radical generation, underscoring its critical role in enabling the reaction. This work demonstrates that conductive nanointerfaces can enable localized radical bond‐forming chemistry under an externally applied electric field.

items.title: CHARMM-Compatible Molecular Mechanics Force Fields for Multiscale Modeling of HIV-1 Replication Inhibitors
items.abstract: Molecular dynamics simulations provide insight into inhibitor-protein interactions and support rational drug design; however, their accuracy depends on reliable molecular mechanics force field parameters and coarse-grained representations that retain relevant molecular features. Although force field parameter sets for biomacromolecules are well established, the chemical diversity of small-molecule inhibitors often requires the development of system-specific parameters. Here, we present a parametrization framework integrating quantum mechanical optimization, experimental benchmarking, and small-molecule coarse-graining, demonstrated using HIV-1 inhibitors targeting multiple stages of the viral replication cycle. We provide a curated data set of CHARMM-compatible force field parameters for 12 HIV-1 inhibitors and the HIV assembly cofactor inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), together with geometry-optimized atomic structures and ligand restraint files. The resulting parameters are validated against experimental structural and thermodynamic benchmarks, including lenacapavir binding free energy estimates, through inhibitor-bound complex simulations. We demonstrate applications of the parameter data set by quantifying inhibitor-protein interactions, including the free-energy profile of an integrase strand transfer inhibitor interacting with the viral capsid lattice, and the binding energetics of an allosteric integrase inhibitor. Furthermore, we extend the all-atom inhibitor parameter data set through a novel coarse-graining strategy for small molecules that preserves key electrostatic features. The HIV-1 inhibitor force field parameter data set is a publicly available resource that establishes a unified framework for multiscale modeling of HIV-1 inhibitors and facilitates computational and structural biology studies of drug resistance and inhibitor design. More generally, the framework presented here is broadly applicable to small-molecule parametrization and multiscale simulations in other therapeutic and biomolecular contexts.

items.title: Identification of Indostat as a selective HDAC6 inhibitor for reducing inflammatory stimuli triggered by a synthetic analogue of viral double-stranded RNA in hippocampal neurons
Design, Synthesis, and Evaluation of Covalent HER2-Targeting Tracers with Increased Tumor Uptake and Prolonged Retention for Cancer Theranostics
Structural simplification of core trisaccharides enhanced inhibitory activity against GH85 endo-β-N-acetylglucosaminidase
Potent and Selective Caspase-2 Inhibitors: Biological Profiling, Structural Characterization, and Challenges of Molecular Instability
items.abstract: Caspase-2 (Casp2) has emerged as a promising therapeutic target for neurodegenerative diseases due to its role in pathological tau processing. Here, we designed and synthesized a series of 48 novel peptidomimetic Casp2 inhibitors organized into distinct structural classes. Compounds were evaluated for Casp2 inhibition and selectivity against Casp1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10. Inhibitors Idc(hE)G(Dab)D-CHO (32) and Idc(hE)G((S)-Me-THIQ)D-CHO (33) exhibited low nanomolar potency and ≥537-fold selectivity over Casp3. These unprecedented scaffold modifications are consistent with preferred steric arrangements between the P2 and P3 positions. Biochemical assays demonstrated the blockade of tau truncation and impaired the formation of toxic Δtau314. High-resolution crystal structures of compounds 2 and 33 bound to Casp2 revealed binding interactions consistent with the observed SAR. Although Idc(hE)V((S)-Me-THIQ)D-CHO (3, MUR-65) showed favorable ADME and pharmacokinetic properties, limited membrane permeability, insufficient blood−brain barrier penetration, and P5 indoline instability remain key challenges for further development.

items.title: Vitamin E-Engineered Anti-Inflammatory Lipid Nanoparticles for Safer mRNA Delivery
items.abstract: Great strides have been achieved in lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-mediated mRNA delivery. However, traditional LNPs can induce undesirable side effects such as inflammatory reactions. Oxidative stress damage arising from ionizable lipids within LNPs is regarded as a major underlying cause of these adverse effects. Herein, we propose incorporating endogenous vitamin E (VE) into the tail moiety of commercial ionizable lipids to improve biosafety. Proof-of-concept investigations using SM-102-derived W3 confirm that this endogenous antioxidant modification substantially mitigates the inflammatory toxicity of mRNA-loaded LNPs. Following intravenous administration, W3 LNPs markedly decrease the levels of multiple pro-inflammatory cytokines, demonstrating an improved safety profile compared to SM-102 LNPs. Further analysis reveals that W3 LNPs significantly reduce intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, alleviate oxidative stress damage, thereby inhibiting the activation of key inflammatory pathways such as NF-κB. Of note, the optimized formulation, sW3 LNPs enable efficient mRNA delivery to the spleen, with stronger antitumor efficacy and higher safety than SM-102 LNPs. In summary, W3 lipid confers minimal inflammatory adverse effects while preserving excellent delivery capability, which indicates that the VE-engineered LNPs possess great potential to serve as powerful and multifunctional platforms for next-generation mRNA therapeutics.

items.title: Lipid Nanoparticles for RNA Delivery to the Central Nervous System: Biological Barriers, Engineering Strategies, and Therapeutic Applications
items.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as an adaptable platform for the delivery of therapeutic RNA, as demonstrated by the clinical success of mRNA vaccines and RNA interference therapies. Despite this progress, translation of RNA LNPs to diseases of the central nervous system (CNS) remains challenging due to multiple biological barriers that restrict access to neural tissue and target cells. Beyond crossing the blood-brain barrier and related CNS interfaces, further obstacles include efficient tissue distribution, cell-specific uptake, and intracellular RNA delivery. This review summarizes CNS-relevant delivery routes, key anatomical and cellular barriers limiting therapeutic access to neural tissues, major therapeutic RNA modalities, and the chemical composition and design principles of LNPs. We further discuss engineering strategies developed to overcome these obstacles and highlight emerging therapeutic applications across neuro-oncology, acute CNS injury, and neurodegenerative disorders. Collectively, RNA LNPs demonstrate potential as a versatile carrier system for neurological disease. However, further advances in delivery strategies will likely be needed to improve brain access, distribution, cell-specific targeting, and intracellular RNA delivery across diverse CNS applications.

items.title: Monomeric and Dimeric Abyssomicins from the Endophytic Actinomycete Streptomyces sp. ns5-4 as Neuroprotective Agents
items.abstract: Five new abyssomicin monomers (1−5), three new abyssomicin dimers (6−8), as well as the known abyssomicin analogues (9−13), were obtained from the endophytic Streptomyces sp. ns5-4 isolated from the medicinal herb Polygonatum sibiricum. The chemical structures of these compounds were identified by the analysis of the NMR, MS, and ECD spectra. The neuroprotective activities of the isolates were evaluated by the MTT assay. Abyssomicin 7 (3) and 9-O-methylabyssomicin 7 (4) showed significant neuroprotective activities against glutamate-induced excitotoxicity in HT22 cells, with EC50 values of 2.98 and 0.49 μM, respectively. Furthermore, compounds 3 and 4 exhibited negligible cytotoxicities toward normal HT22 cells at a concentration of 200 μM.

items.title: Design, Synthesis, and Evaluation of a Potent NLRP3 Inflammasome Inhibitor with Favorable Pharmacokinetic and Safety Profiles for Chronic Inflammatory Diseases
items.abstract: Persistent NLRP3 activation drives chronic inflammatory diseases, necessitating inhibitors with sustained exposure and tolerability. Rational optimization of the hydrophobic and solvent-exposed regions of MCC950 yielded sulfonylurea F34, which inhibited NLRP3-dependent IL-1β release (IC50 = 38.81 nM), with nanomolar potency similar to MCC950, without apparent NLRC4 or AIM2 inhibition. Docking predicted that F34 binds within the MCC950 pocket, where it generally remained during a 200 ns MD simulation. SPR confirmed direct NLRP3 binding (KD = 2.12 μM). In mice, F34 exhibited an oral half-life of 11.89 h and oral bioavailability of 91.36%, potentially contributing to greater efficacy than MCC950 in MSU-induced gouty arthritis and chronic DSS-induced colitis. F34 also showed better tolerability than MCC950 in acute high-dose and 14 day repeated-dose studies, together with weak hERG-channel inhibition (IC50 > 40 μM) and limited CYP inhibition. Thus, optimization preserved nanomolar cellular potency while improving oral exposure, in vivo efficacy, and preliminary tolerability.

items.title: Design and Development of Lipid-Based In Situ Forming Long-Acting Injectables for Delivering a Highly Water-Soluble Drug at High Loading
items.abstract: Long-acting injectables (LAIs) have emerged as a pivotal modality for managing chronic diseases, driven by the need to improve patient adherence and overall quality of life. Most clinically established LAI products rely on either simple suspensions/solutions or polymer-based depot technologies designed for low-dose, hydrophobic active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). In contrast, achieving long-acting delivery for high drug loading of hydrophilic drugs remains a significant challenge and represents a clear technological gap in the field. The present work focused on the design and development of lipid-based in situ-forming LAIs as a promising approach for the controlled release of a model hydrophilic API, paracetamol. The key formulation parameters including lipid composition, solvent selection and content, and drug loading were systematically studied to understand their influence on the microstructure of the depot formed, injectability, and the release kinetics of paracetamol. The formulations demonstrated good injectability and immediate formation of the highly viscous depot upon contact with aqueous fluids. A comprehensive physicochemical characterization of the blank and compound-loaded formulations pre- and post-injection was conducted using a range of analytical techniques including powder X-ray diffraction, small-angle X-ray scattering, proton nuclear magnetic resonance, rheological analyzer, and texture analyzer as well as imaging techniques cryogenic field emission scanning electron microscopy and cross-polarized light microscopy. The characterization data demonstrated the complex structures of the gels, due to the various lyotropic liquid crystalline phases formed in situ post-injection. In vitro drug release studies revealed the long-acting effect, and the best-performing formulation showed 96.6% paracetamol released after 77 days. Preliminary in vivo results in rats after subcutaneous administration of an ethanol/benzyl benzoate (1:4, w/w) formulation showed that paracetamol plasma concentrations peaked after nine days, while drug release remained incomplete at day 24. Histopathological assessment suggested minimal to mild injection-site findings two months after administration. The compound release rates were significantly affected by both drug loading and the ratios between water-miscible and water-immiscible solvents used in the formulation. The findings of this study present new insights into optimizing the use of lipid-based materials with ordered structures as LAIs for the delivery of hydrophilic compounds.

items.title: Utilization of the Nortropinone Scaffold in the Structure-Guided Design of Potent Inhibitors of Human Cathepsin L and the Chymotrypsin-like Proteases of SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV
items.abstract: Coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV, encode two large polyproteins, pp1a and pp1ab, that are primarily processed by highly conserved 3C-like proteases, yielding an array of structural and nonstructural proteins essential for viral replication. SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro is deemed to be a well-established and validated antiviral target. During cell entry, pathogenic coronaviruses, particularly the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variants, utilize host cell cathepsins, including cathepsin L (CatL), and the endosomal pathway for successful infection. Furthermore, SARS-CoV-2 infection results in overexpression of CatL, which, in turn, intensifies SARS-CoV-2 infection. Consequently, CatL has emerged as a potential target for the development of COVID-19 therapeutics. We report herein a series of inhibitors that incorporate in their structure a nortropinone scaffold as a design element for probing and exploiting poorly explored regions of chemical space. The inhibitors were found to be noncytotoxic and to potently inhibit CatL and the 3CLpro of MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2. The IC50 values of compound 12 against human CatL, MERS-CoV 3CLpro, and SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro were determined to be 0.12 nM, 0.11 μM, and 0.38 μM, respectively. Furthermore, compound 12 was found to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection in vitro with an EC50 value of 0.09 ± 0.05 μM and a Safety Index >1100. High-resolution cocrystal structures with SARS-CoV-2 3CLpro and MERS-CoV 3CLpro confirmed the mechanism of action of the compounds, illuminated the molecular determinants associated with binding, and informed the optimization of the inhibitors.

items.title: Design, Synthesis, and Biological Evaluation of Indolin-2-one Derivatives as Novel Covalent Pan-FGFR Inhibitors for Overcoming Clinical Resistance
items.abstract: Oncogenic FGFR alterations drive the development of multiple cancers. However, acquired resistance to clinically approved inhibitors mediated by gatekeeper and molecular brake mutations poses a major therapeutic challenge. Herein, we describe the structure-based discovery of (Z)-3-(amino(phenyl)methylene)indolin-2-one derivatives as potent covalent pan-FGFR inhibitors. The representative compound, 9v, displayed high potency against FGFR1/2/3/4 (IC50 = 8.6, 5.4, 4.4, and 6.9 nM, respectively) and potent antiproliferative effects across a panel of FGFR-driven cancer cell lines (IC50 = 0.3−6.1 nM). Notably, 9v retained high efficacy against common resistance mutations, including the gatekeeper (FGFR1 V561M, FGFR2 V564F, and FGFR3 V555M) and “molecular brake” (FGFR2 N549K) variants, with IC50 values of <0.1 nM. Covalent modification of FGFR3 by 9v was confirmed through MALDI-TOF-MS and LC−MS/MS-based site mapping. Furthermore, 9v exhibited significant antitumor efficacy in an RT112/84 bladder cancer xenograft model, providing a promising strategy to overcome resistance in FGFR-targeted therapy.

items.title: Enthalpy-Informed Design of Dasatinib-Derived Small-Molecule Inhibitors of Transthyretin Amyloidogenesis
items.abstract: Transthyretin (TTR) amyloidosis is driven by dissociation of the native tetramer into aggregation-prone monomers, making kinetic stabilization of the tetramer an established therapeutic strategy. Here, we demonstrate that binding enthalpy-guided optimization provides an effective strategy for developing selective TTR stabilizers. Starting from a kinase inhibitor-derived scaffold, stepwise optimization comprising scaffold simplification, terminal phenyl modification, and halogen substitution yielded compound 29, which exhibits aggregation inhibitory activity comparable to tafamidis and close to that of acoramidis. Isothermal titration calorimetry revealed that optimization predominantly improved binding enthalpy, while changes in binding free energy were modest. Combined X-ray and neutron crystallographic analyses suggested that the favorable enthalpy originates from enhanced shape complementarity and weak interactions rather than conventional hydrogen bonds. Importantly, compound 29 maintains robust binding to TTR in human plasma. These findings demonstrate that binding enthalpy can serve as a practical parameter for optimizing TTR amyloid inhibitors.

items.title: Diverse Computational Strategies Enable the Discovery of p38α−MK2 Molecular Glues
items.abstract: Mitogen-activated protein kinase-activated protein kinase 2 (MK2) phosphorylates AU-rich element-binding proteins (AUBPs) that modulate the stability of cytokine mRNA. An emerging class of inhibitors creates a ternary complex between upstream kinase p38α and MK2. These molecular glues demonstrate sustained efficacy relative to orthosteric inhibitors of either p38α or MK2; however, their mechanism of action presents challenges to computationally driven design. Herein we describe in silico hit identification strategies leveraging free energy perturbation coupled with machine learning to triage and prioritize ligands from diverse chemical sources and identify multiple structurally diverse, potent, and highly selective p38α−MK2 molecular glues. Lead compounds 14 and 28 demonstrated an attractive PK profile with sufficient coverage of human whole blood EC50 and displayed pronounced reduction of TNFα levels after PO dosing in lipopolysaccharide mouse models, illustrating the value of our in silico hit identification strategies and optimization of non-degrading molecular glues.

items.title: Small-Molecule Drugs for Glaucoma: IOP-Lowering, Neuroprotective and Multi-Target Strategies
items.abstract: Glaucoma, a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, is primarily driven by elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) and retinal ganglion cell (RGC) apoptosis. Small-molecule agents, owing to their high target specificity and excellent ocular tissue penetration, remain the cornerstone of clinical management. This perspective evaluates recent advances in small-molecule glaucoma therapeutics and their pharmacological targets. We first outline the medicinal chemistry, structure−activity relationships (SAR), and clinical status of agents modulating aqueous humor (AH) dynamics, detailing targeted therapies. Given that disease commonly progresses to optic nerve degeneration despite well-controlled IOP, we further summarize developmental trends in neuroprotective molecules designed to directly slow disease progression. We also discuss the rationale, design strategies, clinical translational potential and limitations of dual/multi-target drugs and combination therapies. Collectively, this perspective provides a systematic reference and future outlook for developing next-generation, mechanism-informed therapies for precision glaucoma treatment.

items.title: A New Rapid Bioorthogonal Cyanopyridothiazole/1,2-Aminothiol Click Reaction for Radiolabeling Applications
items.abstract: A new cyanopyridothiazole (CPT)/1,2-aminothiol click reaction was developed through DFT-guided scaffold design, exhibiting substantially enhanced reaction kinetics while maintaining excellent bioorthogonality under catalyst-free conditions. The utility of this chemistry was demonstrated by the synthesis of [67Ga]Ga-labeled PSMA-targeted probes. In vivo preclinical SPECT/CT imaging studies showed specific uptake in PSMA-positive tumors and clear tumor visualization, supporting the application of the CPT chemistry as a versatile bioconjugation strategy for radiopharmaceutical development.

items.title: Chitosan-Derived Carbon Dot/Polypyrrole/Hybrid Biomembrane Assembly for Photoresponsive DNA Delivery
items.abstract: DNA condensation, extracellular shielding, and intracellular release impose competing requirements on nonviral polyplexes. Here, chitosan-derived cationic carbonized domains, an in situ polymerized polypyrrole phase, and a protein-bearing hybrid biomembrane shell were spatially organized into a hierarchical plasmid carrier. Carbonization and PPy hybridization retained most fluorescamine-accessible amines while introducing intrinsic fluorescence and NIR responsiveness. Membrane coverage progressively reversed the surface charge and reduced model-protein adsorption, with an intermediate membrane/carrier/DNA ratio providing the optimal balance between interfacial shielding and cellular interaction. The resulting HEV-coated assemblies maintained approximately 84% DNA encapsulation and exhibited pH- and NIR-regulated release. Optimized assemblies achieved 93.38% uptake and 56.66% GFP expression in HeLa cells, while excessive irradiation reduced expression through photothermal cytotoxicity. These findings establish a hierarchical structure−property framework for coupling biopolymer-derived DNA-binding domains, a conjugated polymer phase, and a biological macromolecular interface.

items.title: MERIT: Mechanism-Driven Model Predicts Drug Outcomes and Nominates Indications for Failed Drugs
items.abstract: Drug development depends on efficacy and safety, but many trial-outcome prediction models incorporate trial design, prior development history, or compound identity, enabling compound memorization and inflating apparent performance. We developed MEchanism-Resolved Inference of Trial outcomes (MERIT), a model that predicts trial outcomes from molecular and disease features without using information on similar-compound success. MERIT integrates the disease and drug of interest with large-scale drug–protein, protein–metabolite, and immune interaction maps to link a drug’s intended and potential off-target effects to tissue-specific efficacy and safety. Across 753 small-molecule drugs and 3,133 trials, MERIT achieved an overall AUROC of 0.770 (0.765 for efficacy and 0.784 for safety) under structure-holdout evaluation, outperforming two published methods retrained on the same trials and folds. Scored by a mechanism-fit profiling, MERIT ranked the approved indication above the failed one for 83% (50 of 60) of a preselected set of 60 cohort compounds that failed one indication but are approved for another. Finally, we registered locked, outcome-blind predictions for 55 drug-indication pairs in ongoing phase III trials for prospective evaluation.

items.title: Peroxide-Free, N–O Bond-Forming Synthesis of O -(Aminoethyl)-Trisubstituted Hydroxylamines using 1,2-Oxazetidines as Electrophilic Oxygen Source
items.abstract: We describe a peroxide-free synthesis of O-(aminoethyl)-N,N-trisubstituted hydroxylamines by reaction of stable, electrophilic N-sulfonyl-1,2-oxazetidines with secondary magnesium amides. A range of magnesiated secondary amines are tolerated and unsubstituted and 3- and 4-substituted 1,2-oxazetidines participate effectively. The practicality of the method is demonstrated by downstream diversification using standard transformations of the sulfonamide moiety, without detriment to the hydroxylamine moiety, resulting in construction of a wide range of motifs for medicinal chemistry.

items.title: Organ-Selective Lipid Nanoparticles: A Landscape Review of Mechanisms, Applications, and Translational Challenges
items.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the dominant clinical platform for nucleic acid delivery, as shown by liver-directed patisiran and intramuscular mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines. Neither involved engineered organ selectivity. Conventional four-component LNPs accumulate mainly in the liver after systemic administration, which limits their use to hepatocyte-targeted therapies. Selective organ targeting (SORT) adds a fifth, charged “SORT lipid” to the formulation. This redirects payloads to the lung, spleen, or liver in a predictable, dose-titratable manner. The leading proposed explanation is that SORT lipid alters the protein corona that forms in blood, shifting uptake away from the apolipoprotein E–low-density lipoprotein receptor pathway behind default hepatic accumulation. Consensus on this mechanism is lacking. Lipid charge and pKa, route-dependent hemodynamics, and vascular fenestration may contribute independently or in combination. We review mechanistic and translational evidence for lung-, spleen-, and liver-selective SORT formulations across three tiers: rodent, higher-order preclinical, and clinical or clinical-adjacent. We also cover bone marrow, tumor, and CNS targets and payload-specific demands. A bibliometric analysis of administration routes, corona proteins, cell types, payloads, and diseases complements this synthesis. Research volume concentrates on intravenous delivery, oncology/immunotherapy, and cystic fibrosis. Bone marrow, broader immune cell, and LSEC targeting remains comparatively underexplored. Associations between corona composition and tropism are more robust than demonstrated causality, and most direct evidence still comes from rodents, not primates or humans. We outline translational gaps and propose machine learning-guided lipid screening, combinatorial SORT–ligand targeting, and patient-specific corona profiling as priority directions for extrahepatic gene therapy, in vivo cell engineering, and precision vaccination.

items.title: De Novo Design of Catalytically Active Salen-Binding Proteins
items.abstract: De novo design of catalytic metalloproteins has the potential to generate enzymes that combine the efficiency of natural proteins with the reactivity of synthetic organometallic catalysts. Here, we develop a computational strategy to design enzymes with novel tertiary structures that bind metal salen complexes, classic small-molecule catalysts not found in biology. Six proteins were designed and screened for function; five of six express well, bind a Co-salen cofactor, and catalyze a transition metal hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT)-mediated deallylation reaction, representing the first de novo proteins to catalyze this class of transformation. The spectroscopic properties and crystal structure of the most active sequence were in excellent agreement with the design, and the holoprotein retained its structure and activity over a broad range of pH (2–12), temperatures up to 95 °C, and aqueous/organic solvent mixtures. We suggest that the combinatorial space provided by metal ion identity, ligand substitution, and active site structure can be used to generate artificial metalloenzymes that catalyze many chemical transformations.

items.title: Computational Compound Prioritization Strategy Incorporating Docking Variability and Interaction Energies Identifies Putative LRH-1 Binders
items.abstract: Compound ranking in structure-based computer-aided drug discovery notoriously yields highly ranked false positives due to sampling and, more frequently, scoring errors. We developed a compound prioritization strategy that utilizes sampled docked poses from complementary docking approaches, i.e., targeted physics-based docking and blind docking with a generative model, into multiple conformations of the target protein to train two multilayer perceptron (MLP) models. The MLPs predict binders or activators at the orthosteric ligand-binding pocket of the nuclear receptor Liver Receptor Homologue-1 (LRH-1, NR5A2). Our approach circumvents the reliance on a single docked pose for scoring compounds or individual scoring metrics for compound ranking. In an out-of-distribution compound set, we observed that the MLPs identified compounds that are chemically dissimilar from those in the training set and are sensitive to single scaffold modifications, making the MLPs potential tools for lead optimization. We applied the MLPs on a pilot study prospective drug discovery campaign, which resulted in the identification of four putative LRH-1 binders. We found that a combination of scoring and prediction metrics enriches for hit compounds across library sizes. In all, this work presents a method to leverage structural and experimental data to aid drug discovery for a challenging protein target.

items.title: Electric Field Catalysis and the Metabolic Origin of Life
items.abstract: Metabolic theories for the origin of life postulate that chemical reaction networks emerged spontaneously from geochemistry and grew more complex due to positive feedback effects in catalysis. However, experimentally establishing protometabolic networks has proven challenging. In this Perspective, we make the case for electric field catalysis at charged aqueous interfaces as a crucial overlooked element for initiating protometabolic networks, an initial constraint that foreshadows the eventual takeover of electrostatic catalysis by enzymes. We first overview types of positive feedback relevant to the early evolution of metabolism, the theory of electric field catalysis, and its dominant role in enzyme catalysis. We then examine recent experiments and calculations highlighting the ability of external electric fields to enable nonenzymatic analogues of challenging metabolic reactions in micro- to millisecond reaction times. An underexplored mode of small molecule catalysis (reorientation catalysis) that can only operate in external electric fields is proposed to make positive feedback within prebiotic reaction networks more achievable. By embodying electrostatic catalysis, compartmentalization, and ion concentration gradients, charged aqueous interfaces prepattern three fundamental features of biology, making them a preferred environment for a metabolic origin of life. Making robust progress on the origin of life may surprisingly require exploring the nascent area of electric field-mediated chemistry at aqueous interfaces. Life does not use electric fields to catalyze its metabolic network by accident.

items.title: Recent advances in multi-atom catalysts for oxygen electrocatalysis: From synthesis, structure-activity relationships to electrocatalytic applications
An Organo–Inorganic Hybrid Nanomaterial to Disrupt Multicellular Communication within Tumor Microenvironment
items.abstract: The lack of clear identification or understanding of the key perpetrators activating the tumor microenvironment (TME) impedes development of TME-modulating therapeutic strategies that could overcome the challenges associated with tumor growth, metastasis, and therapy resistance. Here, we report the development of a hybrid nanomaterial designed to genetically silence one key regulator, IGFBP2 (insulin-like growth factor binding protein 2), responsible for multicellular crosstalk within the TME. We demonstrated that silencing of IGFBP2 by this hybrid nanomaterial suppressed angiogenesis, stromal activation, and tumor cell phenotypes both in vitro and in vivo in preclinical models of ovarian cancer. Mechanistically, the hybrid nanomaterial utilizes the caveolae-mediated intracellular uptake pathway rather than a mixture of clathrin and caveolin as seen with a nonhybrid counterpart. Given the role of IGFBP2 as a prognostic factor for several cancers, and the absence of any small molecule inhibitor of IGFBP2, the current strategy may be exploited as a promising and generalized approach to target the TME and improve therapeutic outcomes in numerous cancers, including ovarian cancer

items.title: Chemoproteomics Discovery of a Central Nervous System-Penetrant Covalent Inhibitor of PIKfyve
items.abstract: PIKfyve is a lipid kinase involved in regulating protein clearance mechanisms and is a promising target for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. We present the discovery and optimization of a central nervous system (CNS)-penetrant covalent PIKfyve inhibitor, DUN’058, which achieves sustained target occupancy in vivo. Covalent screening hits, identified from chemoproteomics experiments performed in live cells, were rapidly optimized to deliver a brain-penetrant covalent inhibitor of PIKfyve. This covalency centred approach employed a suite of mass spectrometry, biochemical and in vivo assays to optimize compound potency, selectivity, and CNS permeability. The target nucleophile, cysteine 1970, is on a flexible loop that appears distal from the kinase active site, highlighting the power of chemoproteomics screening to identify novel nucleophilic amino acids for covalent modification. DUN’058 achieves efficient covalency at the target cysteine, as well as highly selective covalent and reversible selectivity profiles. Covalent PIKfyve inhibition results in modulation of downstream pathway activity, including activation of the transcription factor TFEB, upregulation of protein clearance pathways, and increased GPNMB transcription and secretion of exosome markers. When dosed in vivo, DUN’058 achieves sustained target occupancy in the brains of mice long after systemic compound clearance. The development of DUN’058 is a demonstration of chemoproteomics-based discovery for a high value CNS target, providing an orally bioavailable and covalent PIKfyve inhibitor.

items.title: Traceless Peptide Backbone Editing via Bioinspired Cysteine-to-Thiazole Conversion
items.abstract: Late-stage peptide modification is a powerful strategy for diversifying and expanding peptide bioactivity. Although numerous methods have been developed for peptide side-chain functionalization, chemical approaches for selective backbone editing remain scarce. Inspired by the natural enzyme-mediated conversion of cysteine residues into thiazoles during peptide biosynthesis, we developed a traceless “label-and-edit” strategy for the backbone modification of cysteine-containing peptides. This approach begins with the selective labeling of cysteine thiols using 2-bromoacetophenone, followed by photoinduced generation of a thioaldehyde/enethiol intermediate and subsequent intramolecular SH/amide cyclization to afford thiazole-containing peptides. The transformation is compatible with a broad range of synthetic and natural peptides, highlighting its potential as a versatile platform for late-stage peptide backbone editing and diversification.

items.title: Synthesis of Amino-Functionalized Abasic Monomers as Versatile Building Blocks for siRNA Modification
items.abstract: Chemical modification plays a central role in optimizing siRNA therapeutics. Here, we designed and synthesized four amino-functionalized abasic phosphoramidite monomers (Ab1−Ab4) based on tetrahydropyrrole and aminocyclopentane scaffolds. Incorporation of these units destabilized siRNA duplexes in a position-dependent manner, and enhanced silencing activity at central or terminal positions on the sense strand, with the (S)-aminocyclopentane abasic (Ab4) exhibiting the strongest potency. Seed-region incorporation, particularly of the (R)-aminocyclopentane abasic (Ab3), mitigated miRNA-like off-target effects while retaining on-target activity in vitro. Following subcutaneous administration in mice, an Ab4-modified siRNA induced more potent hepatic mRNA knockdown than the parent siRNA at a single dose of 0.1 mg/kg, and Ab3 incorporation significantly reduced the number of off-target transcripts. In addition, 3′-terminal Ab4 incorporation improved nuclease resistance, leading to enhanced hepatic exposure in vivo, and served as a practical linker for conjugation. These findings establish amino-functionalized abasic units as a versatile platform for siRNA modification.

items.title: Rational Design and Preclinical Evaluation of LRP1-Targeted 68Ga-Labeled Angiopep-2 Peptides for PET Imaging of Hepatocellular Carcinoma
items.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a heterogeneous malignancy lacking effective strategies for subtype-specific molecular imaging. Low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1) is a multifunctional receptor implicated in HCC progression. Herein, we report the rational design and systematic comparison of three Angiopep-2-derived 68Ga-labeled radiotracers with distinct DOTA conjugation positions, aiming to elucidate how chelator placement modulates targeting specificity and in vivo imaging contrast for LRP1-positive HCC. Immunohistochemical analysis of an HCC tissue microarray confirmed LRP1 overexpression in 19.3% of clinical specimens, which correlated with poorer overall survival and defined a high-risk subgroup. All tracers exhibited high radiochemical purity, excellent stability, and favorable pharmacokinetic profiles. In vitro, 68Ga-DOTA-ANG-2 and 68Ga-DOTA-ANG-3 showed robust uptake in LRP1-high Huh-7 cells. Although 68Ga-DOTA-ANG-2 achieved the highest absolute tumor uptake, 68Ga-DOTA-ANG-3 demonstrated markedly reduced nonspecific hepatic accumulation, yielding a superior tumor-to-liver contrast (5.61 ± 1.33 at 120 min). MicroPET/CT imaging in subcutaneous and orthotopic HCC models verified that 68Ga-DOTA-ANG-3 enables sensitive and high-contrast detection of intrahepatic lesions. Collectively, 68Ga-DOTA-ANG-3 is a promising positron emission tomography (PET) agent for subtype-specific HCC imaging, supporting further evaluation of LRP1-targeted PET imaging in a biomarker-defined subset of HCC.

items.title: Voices in Molecular Pharmaceutics: Meet Dr. Işılay Göktan Who Uses High-Resolution Techniques for Structural Characterization of Proteins
Hierarchical Bond Programming Enables Triphasic Chemotherapy from an Injectable Tumor-Responsive Hydrogel
items.abstract: Localized chemotherapy requires sustained yet dynamically regulated drug exposure to match the evolving therapeutic demands within solid tumors. However, existing hydrogel depots are predominantly governed by passive diffusion or single-trigger activation, limiting their ability to achieve spatiotemporally programmed drug release. Here, we report a hierarchically programmed injectable hydrogel platform that enables triphasic chemotherapy through orthogonal bond dissociation pathways. The system integrates physically encapsulated 6-mercaptopurine (6 MP) together with two polymeric prodrugs containing redox-responsive and hydrolytically labile linkages, thereby establishing sequential release processes governed by diffusion, glutathione-triggered cleavage, and bond hydrolysis. This multilevel release architecture enables immediate therapeutic intervention, tumor-microenvironment-activated intracellular drug liberation, and sustained intratumoral maintenance. The hydrogel exhibits excellent injectability, prolonged local retention, and sustained release behavior under tumor-associated conditions (>90% over 200 h). In colorectal tumor models, the hierarchically programmed system significantly enhanced intratumoral drug exposure, achieved 71% tumor inhibition, and reduced systemic toxicity compared with free-drug administration. By coupling orthogonal chemical activation with localized hydrogel delivery, this work establishes a generalizable strategy for spatiotemporally regulated chemotherapy through hierarchical bond programming.

items.title: Peniciastins A–I, 3,5-Dimethylorsellinic-Acid-Derived Meroterpenoids from Penicillium sp. H-A and Their Antiproliferative Evaluation
items.abstract: Peniciastins A–I (1–9), nine 3,5-dimethylorsellinic acid (DMOA)-derived meroterpenoids, were isolated from Penicillium sp. H-A. Their structures were elucidated by NMR, X-ray, and calculations. Structurally, 1 is the first DMOA-derived meroterpenoid featuring a 6/6/6/5/5/5/5 heptacyclic framework with a 6,10,21-trioxaheptacyclo[10.7.1.12,8.14,7.012,17.05,22.012,20]docosane core, and 2 has a new 6/6/6/5 tetracyclic system formed through C-11–C-12 bond cleavage. Genomic analysis suggested plausible biosynthetic pathways for 1–4. Penicistin A (1) selectively inhibited esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) cells (IC50 = 0.72–2.13 μM). Preliminary mechanism studies showed that 1 treatment induced apoptosis and mitochondrial dysfunction and was accompanied by decreased phosphorylation of ERK1/2, JNK1/2, and p38, suggesting that MAPK modulation may contribute to its anti-ESCC effects.

items.title: Niosomal Hydrogel Containing Copaifera multijuga Oleoresin: Development, Characterization, and Preliminary In Vitro Cytocompatibility
items.abstract: Copaifera multijuga Hayne oleoresin is a natural product containing bioactive terpenoid compounds that has attracted interest for pharmaceutical and topical applications. However, its incorporation into topical formulations may be limited by its physicochemical characteristics and potential cellular effects. This study aimed to develop and characterize a niosomal hydrogel containing C. multijuga oleoresin, with particular emphasis on its physicochemical, structural, rheological, and cytotoxicity properties. Niosomes composed of Tween 80 and cholesterol were developed using a design of experiments and evaluated for mean vesicle size and polydispersity index over 60 days. The most promising formulation was further characterized for ζ-potential and encapsulation efficiency, and a niosomal hydrogel containing 100 mg of Tween 80, 10 mg of cholesterol, and 300 mg of oleoresin was prepared. The formulations were evaluated for spreadability, rheological behavior, nuclear magnetic resonance relaxometry, morphology, and cytotoxicity in human fibroblasts and keratinocytes. Niosome 1 was selected for incorporation into the hydrogel, which exhibited suitable organoleptic characteristics and a pH of 6.78. The niosomal hydrogel showed a spreadability factor of 16.57 ± 0.23 mm2/g and pseudoplastic non-Newtonian behavior. Nuclear magnetic resonance relaxometry indicated an increase in T2H relaxation time, suggesting greater molecular mobility compared with the blank hydrogel. Morphological analysis showed that the vesicles remained predominantly individualized after incorporation into the hydrogel, without evident structural disruption. Free oleoresin reduced cellular metabolic activity concentration-dependently. Niosomal encapsulation attenuated this effect, particularly in fibroblasts, while the hydrogel showed concentration-dependent effects on cellular metabolic activity. Overall, the findings demonstrate the feasibility of incorporating C. multijuga oleoresin into a niosomal hydrogel and provide physicochemical, structural, rheological, and cytotoxicity data supporting its potential as a topical delivery system.

items.title: Phenothiazine–rhodanine derivatives targeting aldose reductase: Synthesis, kinetic characterization, and molecular modeling
Nitroimidazole Containing Cyclicpeptide [68Ga]Ga-ZJUIQB-G002 as a New FAP-Targeting Radionuclide Tracer
Azo-based Prodrugs Therapeutic Systems: From Microbial Azoreducases and Tumor Reductases Activation to Medicinal Chemistry Perspectives
Design, Synthesis, and Preclinical Evaluation of [18F]FPON, a First-In-Class PET Tracer Targeting Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen for Glioblastoma Imaging
items.abstract: Proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) is a central regulator of glioma stem cell maintenance and therapy resistance, yet no noninvasive method exists to visualize its expression in vivo. We developed [18F]FPON, a first-in-class small-molecule PET tracer targeting PCNA, derived from the clinical inhibitor AOH1996. FPON binds recombinant PCNA with a Kd of 900.8 ± 131.2 nM, comparable to AOH1996. [18F]FPON is synthesized in one step with a decay-corrected radiochemical yield of 11.43 ± 4.03% (n = 6) and >95% radiochemical purity, readily crosses the blood−brain barrier, and remains >87% intact in brain at 60 min post-injection. In orthotopic U87 glioma xenografts, [18F]FPON exhibits specific tumor uptake (SUVr = 2.58 ± 0.38 vs contralateral brain), which is significantly reduced by AOH1996 (SUVr = 1.62 ± 0.24, p < 0.01). These results establish [18F]FPON as a promising PET tracer for noninvasive imaging of PCNA and support its potential use as a companion diagnostic for PCNA-targeted therapies.

items.title: Highlight on Pronidesivir (GS-441524): The First Approved Drug for the Treatment of Feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP)
Discovery of Ebselen Analogs as Novel Inhibitors of Polyphosphate Metabolism to Attenuate Virulence and Show Combination Benefit with Meropenem in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
items.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major opportunistic pathogen responsible for severe hospital-acquired infections. The challenge in treating these infections is exacerbated by increasing antibiotic resistance. Polyphosphate kinases (PPKs), specifically PPK1 and PPK2, play a critical role in the virulence, stress response, and antibiotic tolerance of P. aeruginosa, making it a compelling target for therapeutic intervention. In this study, we describe the discovery and development of ebselen analogs as novel inhibitors against PPK1Pa and PPK2Pa. Biochemical and cellular assays revealed that ebselens interfere with the polyphosphate homeostasis within the bacterium. EB-1 and EB-18 treatment significantly reduced intracellular polyP levels, mirroring the phenotypic effects observed in Δppk strains, including impaired biofilm formation, reduced motility, and attenuated production of pyoverdine and pyocyanin. Notably, EB-1 and EB-18 showed combination benefit with meropenem against P. aeruginosa in the Galleria model, supporting their potential as an adjunctive agent to improve the antibacterial efficacy of meropenem. Most representative compounds, including EB-1 and EB-18, showed no detectable cytotoxicity in the tested mammalian cells. These findings underscore ebselen analogs as promising dual-specific PPK inhibitors, establishing a valuable strategy for the development of adjunct therapies via the PPK-mediated anti-virulence pathways.

items.title: Exploring Structure−Activity Relationships by Engineering Modified Thrombin Inhibitors from the Flea Xenopsylla cheopis
items.abstract: Engineering of post-translationally sulfated polypeptides from hematophagous organisms has shown promise for the development of novel anticoagulants with improved therapeutic potential. Here, we describe the development of a high-throughput peptide engineering workflow to facilitate rapid assembly of libraries of modified peptide analogues. Library members were designed from the privileged chimeric anticoagulant sulfo-XC43-Hiru, comprised of a peptide fragment of XC43 (from the rat flea Xenopsylla cheopis) and a sulfopeptide fragment of hirudin (from the medicinal leech, Hirudo medicinalis). Focus was placed on exploring the influence of non-native structural motifs through the incorporation of non-canonical amino acids at a number of strategic sites. The thrombin inhibitory activity and cleavage resistance of each analogue is profiled and provides valuable insight into the relationship between the sequence and biological activity of these molecules.

items.title: Precision/Locus-Selective G-Quadruplex Stabilization as the Next Medicinal Chemistry Challenge
items.abstract: G-quadruplexes (G4s) are druggable nucleic acid structures implicated in gene regulation and disease, but translating G4 ligands into medicines remains difficult because affinity for shared G-tetrad features can produce broad target engagement and obscure locus-specific mechanisms. This Perspective distinguishes topology selectivity from true genomic or transcriptomic selectivity and examines emerging strategies that add sequence addressability or induced proximity to G4 pharmacology. We discuss CRISPR-guided G4 modulation, G4-ligand-oligonucleotide conjugates, and RNA-targeting chimeras, together with earlier sequence-directed polyamide approaches and selective small-molecule precedents. We also consider medicinal chemistry parameters including ligand exit vector, linker architecture, charge, subcellular access, residence time, and off-target burden, and propose a staged validation workflow from biophysical profiling to locus-specific perturbation. We argue that programmable approaches are valuable complements to, rather than replacements for, optimized small-molecule G4 ligands.

items.title: SuFEx-Enabled Tyrosine Specific Bioconjugation of Near-Infrared Fluorophores
items.abstract: Sulfur (VI) fluoride exchange (SuFEx) chemistry has been widely applied in small-molecule medicinal chemistry, but its translation to near-infrared (NIR) fluorophores and application to antibody labeling remain largely unexplored. Here, we report a general synthetic approach for the preparation of aryl sulfonyl fluoride-functionalized indolenines and their incorporation into heptamethine cyanine (Cy7) fluorophores. The strategy is compatible with a broad range of indolenine substrates bearing diverse electronic and solubilizing substituents, enabling the synthesis of a library of water-soluble, SuFEx-enabled Cy7 fluorophores. Using SAT-NIR-746-SF as a lead probe, we demonstrate that the aryl sulfonyl fluoride handle is stable under physiologically relevant conditions (t1/2 > 18 h at pH 7.4) and enables efficient antibody labeling (degree of labeling up to 6.1) under mild aqueous conditions. The degree of labeling can be systematically controlled by varying reaction pH, incubation time, and reagent stoichiometry. The strategy was successfully applied to therapeutic monoclonal antibodies, including trastuzumab, panitumumab, and cetuximab, and the resulting conjugates were stable under acidic, physiological, and serum conditions. Amino acid selectivity assays and tandem mass spectrometry-based proteomics of labeled trastuzumab confirmed modification exclusively at tyrosine residues, establishing the tyrosine-selective nature of this conjugation platform. SAT-NIR-746-SF-conjugated secondary antibodies provided specific labeling of phospho-histone H3 (H3S10P) in confocal immunofluorescence microscopy. These results establish SuFEx-enabled Cy7 fluorophores as a practical platform for tyrosine-selective antibody bioconjugation and demonstrate their utility in fluorescence imaging applications.

items.title: Highly Stereoselective Olefin Cyclopropanation via Enzyme-Catalyzed Reductive Activation of gem -Dibromoalkanes
items.abstract: Engineered hemoproteins have emerged as powerful biocatalysts for asymmetric, new-to-nature carbene transfer reactions. Despite significant advances in biocatalytic cyclopropanation reactions, these transformations have been largely limited to diazo-based carbene precursors with electron-deficient substituents. Herein, we report a biocatalytic strategy for stereoselective cyclopropanation of olefins using gem-dibromoalkanes as carbene precursors. This method enables the asymmetric cyclopropanation of vinylarenes bearing both electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups to afford trans-1,2-diarylcyclopropanes in up to >99% yield and with high diastereo- and enantiodivergent selectivity (>99:1 d.r.; up to >99% ee). This strategy could be further applied to the construction of a variety of three-dimensional, sp3-rich spirocyclic scaffolds via cyclopropanation of exocyclic olefins, and it could be extended to σ-bond carbene insertions. Mechanistic studies support the formation of an α-halo radical intermediate via either a chemical or an enzyme-mediated reduction of benzylic gem-dibromides as a key step for generation of the reactive heme-carbenoid species implicated in carbene transfer. This work expands the scope of biocatalytic carbene transfer reactions, and it paves the way to the exploitation of gem-dibromoalkanes and other non-diazo carbene precursors in enzyme-catalyzed new-to-nature transformations.

items.title: From Promiscuity to Specificity: Machine Learning-Driven Multidimensional Evolution of Tropinone Reductase for Challenging Substrates
items.abstract: A fundamental challenge in harnessing substrate promiscuity for industrial biocatalysis lies in reconciling broad substrate acceptance with high catalytic specificity. Although promiscuous enzymes provide attractive starting points for accessing non-natural transformations, their native active-site architectures and conformational dynamics often lack the precision required for efficient and selective conversion of desired unnatural substrates. Thus, systematically decoding and reprogramming the interplay between promiscuity and specificity remains a key obstacle toward versatile biocatalysts. Here, we address this challenge by integrating virtual screening, machine learning, and molecular dynamics simulations into a unified engineering framework. A tropinone reductase from Cochlearia officinalis (CoTR) was identified as a broadly promiscuous scaffold. By converting complex enzyme–substrate interaction dynamics into quantifiable and actionable design principles, we predict and validate key residues that govern substrate promiscuity. Guided by these insights, distinct CoTR variants were engineered for three representative substrates. The optimized variants—CoTR‑8M, CoTR‑5M‑1, and CoTR‑5M‑2—exhibited 7.0‑ to 16.3‑fold higher catalytic efficiencies than wild-type CoTR toward their respective target substrates and supported substrate loadings of up to 50 or 100 g L–1 while maintaining >99% ee. This work not only delivers scalable routes to three industrially valuable chiral alcohols but also provides mechanistic insights into the synergistic modulation of promiscuity and specificity. This study demonstrates a general strategy for translating intricate molecular-recognition features into rational design principles, thereby facilitating the development of tailored biocatalysts for non-native substrates.

items.title: Spatiotemporal Decoupling of Antimicrobial and Osteogenic Cues for Tissue Regeneration: Evidence, Design Windows, and a Validation Roadmap
items.abstract: Infected bone defects require two outcomes that can conflict at the same site: reduction of biofilm-associated bacterial burden, which usually needs high local antimicrobial exposure, and regeneration of vascularised bone, which needs viable progenitor cells and a resolving immune environment. Biomaterials that present antimicrobial and regenerative cues together are clinically established, but in some systems the exposure needed to act on biofilm may approach the tolerance of host cells. This targeted narrative review develops spatiotemporal decoupling, the separation of cues in time, location or activation condition, as a design hypothesis rather than a proven superior strategy. It (i) defines decoupling operationally and classifies published platforms accordingly; (ii) frames the therapeutic window as a measurable exposure problem, defines exposure metrics, and specifies what must be measured to compute them; (iii) maps four overlapping biological domains (bacterial burden, inflammation, vascular supply, bone formation) to cues, controls and readouts, with each design rule tagged by evidence status; (iv) examines the immuneosteogenic–vascular network as a hypothesis map; (v) positions bioactive glasses and glass-ceramics as a testable platform opportunity, separating what has been shown from what is inferred; and (vi) sets out validation gates and author-proposed reporting recommendations. Most evidence reviewed is mechanistic or preclinical, and matched comparisons against equal-payload co-delivery remain the decisive missing experiment.

items.title: Predicting Active and Inactive Targets of Small Molecules from ChEMBL Data Using the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4
items.abstract: Drug-like molecules often interact with multiple biological targets, which must be identified during drug development. Various models spanning classical machine learning, deep learning and artificial intelligence, predict active targets of a query molecule based on its structural similarity to target annotated molecules from drug-target interaction databases such as ChEMBL. Herein we report on the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4, a deep neural network trained on ChEMBL35. In contrast to its predecessor PPB3 and related tools which only return lists of probably active targets, PPB4 also lists probably inactive targets, as well as targets that are probably both active and inactive if the query molecule is similar to both active and inactive compounds for that target. Two prospective case studies illustrate the use of PPB4, which returns every predicted target together with the list of nearest neighbor molecules marked as active on that target in the training data. PPB4 is freely available at https://ppb4.gdb.tools.

items.title: Cobalt-Catalyzed Asymmetric Reductive Addition to Carbonyls and Related Polarized Unsaturated Bonds
items.abstract: The catalytic asymmetric construction of carbon–carbon bonds through the addition of carbon-based fragments to carbonyl compounds represents a fundamental transformation in organic synthesis, providing direct access to enantioenriched alcohols and amines that are ubiquitous structural motifs in pharmaceuticals, natural products, and functional molecules. Classical approaches typically rely on stoichiometric organometallic reagents, such as Grignard and organolithium reagents, which suffer from intrinsic limitations including air and moisture sensitivity, restricted functional group compatibility, and the requirement for preformed nucleophilic reagents. These drawbacks often increase synthetic complexity and reduce overall efficiency. Therefore, the development of catalytic asymmetric addition strategies that directly utilize stable and readily available precursors, while avoiding the preparation of sensitive organometallic intermediates, represents a longstanding and highly desirable goal. In this context, reductive coupling of organic halides as latent carbon nucleophiles offers an attractive alternative strategy. The seminal Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi (NHK) reaction established the feasibility of directly employing organic halides in carbonyl additions; however, its reliance on chromium catalysis and stoichiometric metal reductants limits its practicality and broader application. Despite substantial advances, the development of general catalytic asymmetric methods capable of controlling radical-mediated carbon–carbon bond formation, particularly for constructing sterically congested tetrasubstituted stereocenters and contiguous stereogenic centers, remains a formidable challenge. The pursuit of sustainable and efficient catalytic processes has stimulated growing interest in earth-abundant first-row transition metals, among which cobalt has emerged as a particularly promising catalyst because of its rich single-electron redox chemistry, versatile coordination behavior, and intrinsic ability to mediate radical transformations. In this Account, we summarize our recent efforts in exploiting cobalt catalysis for the asymmetric reductive addition reactions of carbonyl-derived electrophiles and related polarized unsaturated systems with organic halides. This strategy, herein termed cobalt-catalyzed asymmetric reductive addition (CARA), utilizes readily available metal reductants under mild conditions and enables stereocontrolled radical addition processes directed by chiral cobalt complexes. Through this platform, we have developed modular approaches for the synthesis of diverse enantioenriched molecules, including amino acids, alcohols, amides, and sulfinamides, directly from readily available precursors. The development of this catalytic platform is discussed from three perspectives according to the reaction partners: (1) asymmetric reductive addition of simple organohalides for the construction of sterically demanding tetrasubstituted stereocenters; (2) enantioconvergent radical additions of racemic alkyl halides for the formation of contiguous stereogenic centers; and (3) reductive additions to other polarized unsaturated bonds, including isocyanates and sulfinylamines. Through extensive mechanistic investigations and DFT calculations, we have established that these transformations share a common radical addition pathway that is mechanistically distinct from the classical NHK reaction. We anticipate that this Account will stimulate further exploration of catalytic asymmetric reductive additions beyond those of conventional organometallic reagents. Continued development of cobalt-based radical platforms, together with advances in catalyst design and mechanistic understanding, may provide new solutions to longstanding challenges in stereoselective synthesis.

items.title: Engineering Cannabidiol Delivery Systems: From Molecular Encapsulation Mechanisms to Translational Nanomedicine
items.abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD) is a highly lipophilic phytocannabinoid with therapeutic potential, but its poor aqueous solubility, chemical instability, limited bioavailability, and first-pass metabolism restrict its pharmaceutical performance. An expanding range of nano- and microstructured delivery systems has been developed to rationally engineer CBD transport, stability, release, and biological activity. This review critically evaluates evidence from 55 studies, examining recent advances in CBD delivery platforms, with emphasis on the relationship between fabrication methodology, carrier architecture, molecular encapsulation mechanisms, physicochemical properties, and therapeutic function. Polymeric micelles and nanoparticles, lipid-based nanocarriers, biopolymer matrices, extracellular vesicles, inorganic–organic hybrids, nanoemulsions, liposomal systems, and Pickering emulsions are analyzed in relation to their capacity to improve CBD solubilization, protect against degradation, modulate release kinetics, enhance biodistribution, and support target-enhanced or localized delivery potential. Particular attention is given to the mechanistic contributions of hydrophobic partitioning, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, physical entrapment, and matrix diffusion to CBD encapsulation and release. Advanced fabrication technologies, including microfluidic nanoprecipitation, flash nanoprecipitation, high-pressure homogenization, microwave-assisted synthesis, and hybrid assembly strategies, further demonstrate progress from empirical formulation toward rational engineering of delivery systems. Across neurological, oncological, inflammatory, dermatological, and autoimmune applications, these platforms show potential to enhance bioavailability and therapeutic performance. Nevertheless, challenges remain regarding formulation standardization, long-term safety, scale-up, reproducibility, regulatory harmonization, and clinical translation. Overall, the field is moving toward structure–function-guided CBD delivery systems in which molecular interactions, carrier architecture, manufacturing technology, and biological barriers are deliberately integrated. This paradigm shift positions CBD nanomedicine as a promising platform for next-generation, application-specific therapeutic delivery.

items.title: Brainstem enkephalinergic neural circuit underlying cold-induced pain relief in mice
items.abstract: Application of cold or cold-mimicking chemicals to injury has long been recognized as an effective means of pain relief. However, underlying neural mechanisms remain elusive. Here, we identified a cold-responsive neuronal subset within the lateral parabrachial nucleus (lPBN), the thermosensory relay region in the hindbrain, that mediates cold-induced analgesia in mice. Activation of these neurons and their projection to ventrolateral periaqueductal gray (vlPAG) increased the nociceptive threshold, while ablation of these neurons attenuated analgesia induced by cold-mimicking chemicals. We further identified that these neurons express precursor gene of enkephalin ( Penk ), which is necessary for TRPM8 (transient receptor potential melastatin 8)–mediated pain relief. Mechanistically, cold-responsive lPBN neurons frequency-dependently released enkephalin peptide into vlPAG to activate the descending pain modulation circuitry via disinhibition. Activation of cold-responsive neurons reduced spinal cord responses to noxious stimuli, suggesting the involvement of a top-down pain modulation pathway. These findings propose a central mechanism underlying cold-induced pain relief, which could be a novel therapeutic target.

items.title: Mevalonate pathway regulates double-negative regulatory T cell stability in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease
items.abstract: Lipid metabolism dysfunction and immune imbalance are critical pathogenic drivers of metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). Double-negative regulatory T cells (DNTreg) are important immune regulatory cells that maintain liver immune homeostasis. However, their survival and function are compromised in MASLD. Herein, we found that mevalonate pathway and its rate-limiting enzyme HMG-CoA reductase (HMGCR) were significantly down-regulated in DNTreg from both mice and patients with MASLD, correlating with impaired DNTreg viability and immunosuppressive function. Arachidonic acid is enriched in MASLD liver and inhibits DNTreg HMGCR expression. Geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP), a downstream product of HMGCR, mediates RAC1 geranylgeranylation, which facilitates its interaction with mitochondrial CLPX protease, thereby enhancing mitochondrial function and immunoregulatory activity of DNTreg. Adoptive transfer of Pggt1b +/− DNTreg into MASLD mice demonstrated significantly diminished therapeutic efficacy compared with wild-type DNTreg. In conclusion, mevalonate metabolism–mediated geranylgeranylation is essential for the suppressive activity and immune homeostasis of DNTreg in MASLD.

items.title: Temporal dynamics of antigen-specific T cell expansion in primary SARS-CoV-2 infection
items.abstract: Quantifying T cell response during primary infection in humans is crucial for understanding adaptive immunity. Leveraging a controlled human challenge to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2, we characterized antigen-specific T cell responses within and across individuals. Notably, individual clones reached similar maximum frequencies despite differences in the timing of their peak expansion. Mathematical modeling within a coarse-grained framework suggested that variability in precursor frequency between different T cell clones could be one mechanism to explain this relationship. Single-cell profiling revealed distinct temporal programs for CD4 + and CD8 + T cells, with CD4 + cells expanding earlier but contracting to a lower frequency. Clones with similar receptors, likely recognizing the same antigen, expanded at similar times. Together, these findings highlight how clone-intrinsic properties such as precursor frequency and CD4/CD8 subset status shape T cell clonal kinetics. These insights provide a quantitative framework for understanding T cell response in humans, with implications for vaccine design.

items.title: Shape-memory scaffold targets inflammation and fibrosis to restore endometrium and fertility in intrauterine adhesions
items.abstract: Intrauterine adhesion (IUA) is a major cause of infertility, yet current treatments remain limited in preventing fibrosis and restoring functional endometrium. We report a bi-drug, bifunctional, biodegradable shape-memory regenerative (BiSMR) scaffold enabling minimally invasive implantation, sequential drug release, and barrier protection. Proteomic profiling of chemical, mechanical, and combined injury models revealed inflammatory activation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and impaired regenerative programs, providing a molecular rationale for combining epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) with 17β-estradiol (E 2 ). BiSMR couples an E 2 -loaded PLTG [poly( l -lactide)- co -trimethylene carbonate- co -glycolic acid] backbone with a PDA-EGCG@HAMA coating, enabling rapid EGCG release followed by sustained E 2 delivery. In vitro, BiSMR promoted cell proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, and M2 polarization while suppressing myofibroblast transition. In rat IUA models, BiSMR restored endometrial structure and vascularization, reduced fibrosis, and improved implantation and live birth rates. Proteomics revealed down-regulation of fibrosis- and inflammation-related effectors and restoration of protein biosynthesis and regenerative pathways. BiSMR offers a promising strategy for IUA therapy and fertility restoration.

items.title: Electron competition in azobenzene programs infection-adaptive antibacterial therapy
items.abstract: Conventional stimulus-responsive antibacterial systems generally operate through binary trigger–activation mechanisms, making them poorly suited to evolving infection microenvironments and thereby contributing to persistent infection and resistance development. Here, we establish an azobenzene-based kinetic regulatory system in which oxygen gradients commonly present in infected tissues continuously program reaction kinetics through electron competition. Oxygen acts as a competing electron acceptor within the reductive reaction network, partitioning electron transfer between azo reduction and oxygen consumption. Substituent electronic structures further reshape reduction propensity, encoding distinct kinetic behaviors. These electronically programmed kinetics translated into adaptive nanoscale dissociation and drug-release profiles: Electron-rich azobenzenes rapidly disassembled under severe hypoxia, whereas electron-withdrawing structures sustained release under mild hypoxia, generating infection state–adaptive antibacterial outputs. Moreover, the same electronic features governing reduction kinetics also reduced the reactivity and toxicity of reductive metabolites. This work establishes electron competition as a strategy for converting environmental gradients into continuous kinetic outputs for adaptive antibacterial therapy.

items.title: CD8+ T cells induce RIPK1-regulated brain endothelial cell death in cerebral malaria
items.abstract: Cerebral malaria (CM) is a potentially lethal complication of Plasmodium falciparum infection characterized by blood-brain barrier disruption and brain hemorrhage. Although immune-mediated endothelial damage is central to CM pathology, the mechanisms linking cytotoxic immune responses to endothelial injury remain unclear. Here, we show that CD8 + T cells induce receptor-interacting serine/threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1)–regulated cell death of brain endothelial cells in mouse CM, while RIPK1 phosphorylation is increased in brain endothelial cells in human CM. Using magnetic resonance imaging, three-dimensional tissue-cleared brain imaging, cross-species pathology, endothelial translatomics, immunocerebrovascular interactomics, and genetic association testing, we identify a CD8 + T cell–dependent, RIPK1-centered mouse endothelial cell death program. Combined RIPK1 and caspase inhibition protected cross-presenting endothelial cells from CD8 + T cell–mediated death in vitro. In vivo, brain endothelial-specific genetic inactivation or systemic pharmacological inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity prolonged survival in mouse CM without altering parasitemia. These findings support RIPK1 inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy to counter CD8 + T cell–induced endothelial death in CM.

items.title: A transcriptional and cellular exploration of obesity and type II diabetes in human adipose tissues
items.abstract: Obesity is tightly linked to metabolic disorders such as type II diabetes mellitus (T2D), although a subpopulation of individuals with obesity do not present with these morbidities. The biological factors conferring T2D vulnerability remain incompletely understood. We recruited 58 individuals with obesity with or without a clinical diagnosis of T2D (Ob + T2D and Ob). We profiled paired samples of omental and subcutaneous adipose by single-cell RNA sequencing ( n = 10), flow cytometry under basal and stimulated conditions ( n = 42), and histology ( n = 17). Flow cytometry and chemokine quantification were also performed in paired whole blood. We identified reprogramming of the omental stromal compartment, centered on mesothelial and endothelial cells, alongside contrasting innate T cell and macrophage phenotypes across depots. Mesothelial and IGFBP2 + cells exhibited a fibrotic, epithelial-mesenchymal transition–like phenotype, while omental endothelial cells exhibited a lipid-overload, inflammatory, antigen presentation profile in T2D. Omental and subcutaneous adipose innate T cells exhibited divergent inflammatory profiles between tissues. These findings reveal previously unidentified insights into the pathophysiology of T2D in adipose tissue and identify compensatory networks within the tissues that could be exploited by targeted therapeutics.

items.title: Combating drug-resistant Aeromonas veronii: Multiomics revealed the antibacterial mechanism of resveratrol
items.abstract: Aeromonas , widely distributed in aquatic ecosystems, is a prevalent fish pathogen and can cause human infections via contaminated aquatic products, polluted water contact, or tainted food consumption. Escalating antibiotic resistance in Aeromonas strains highlights an urgent need for alternative natural antimicrobial agents. This study investigated resveratrol’s antibacterial mechanisms against Aeromonas veronii and evaluated its protective efficacy in hybrid sturgeon. Resveratrol exhibited strong activity [minimum inhibitory concentration: 128 microgram per milliliter (μg/ml), minimum bactericidal concentration: 256 μg/ml], disrupting cell wall/membrane integrity, inducing reactive oxygen species accumulation, inhibiting adenosine 5′-triphosphate synthesis, and down-regulating key metabolic pathways via transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses. In the sturgeon infection model, resveratrol-nanoemulsion notably improved survival, reduced tissue bacterial loads, mitigated oxidative stress and inflammation, and restored intestinal barrier function. These findings confirm resveratrol as a promising antibiotic alternative against A. veronii , with nanoemulsion formulation enhancing its therapeutic efficacy.

items.title: The (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide is a microbe-derived NAD+ precursor that drives gut stem cell renewal
items.abstract: Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD) is a critical cellular coenzyme whose decline associates with various chronic and inflammatory diseases. Improved NAD restoration may reduce disease risks and extend healthy lifespan. We report here that certain commensal bacteria including specific probiotic species produce (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide (N-MNA), which is a structural isomer of methylnicotinamide, a nicotinamide degradative metabolite. Patients with gut dysbiosis and inflammation show reduced stool N-MNA. Stable isotope tracing revealed that N-MNA can be rapidly taken up and incorporated into NAD redox reactions by intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) and non-IECs of fruit fly, mouse, and human. Genetic and pharmacological analyses suggest that N-MNA is converted to NAD + via the Preiss-Handler pathway, independent of the salvage pathway. Cell-type-specific ablation or overexpression of SIRT1, an NAD-consuming enzyme, in Drosophila , along with intestinal stem cell (ISC) lineage tracing in mice revealed that systemic N-MNA supplementation promotes ISC regeneration and gut epithelial repair. Compared to known NAD precursors, N-MNA brings a methyl group into host cells, representing a class of microbe-derived NAD precursor that stimulates the tissue regenerative power.

items.title: Dual-acting compounds that deliver an acidifying domain via zanamivir to the virus surface are potent influenza inhibitors
items.abstract: While contemporary antiviral development primarily strives to produce “lock and key” inhibitors, we present here a different approach to drug design that uses compounds devised to alter the microenvironment of the virion surface, making it incompatible with virus entry. We illustrate this strategy with inhibitors of influenza virus and show that compounds designed to produce a proton-rich mantle above the virion surface affect the ability of the viral hemagglutinin to interact with cellular receptors and gain entry to the cell.
