Selective Nformylation was achieved with formyl–pivalic mixed anhydride under Schotten–Baumann conditions, providing UDP-4-deoxy-4formamido-α-L-arabinose (UDP-Ara4FN, 72%). These results demonstrate that despite the presence of multiple nucleophilic functionalities, chemoselective amine functionalization can be achieved on fully deprotected NDP amino sugars, providing a practical approach to accessing functionalized nucleotide sugar analogues.

items.title: Structure-based virtual screening, in vitro and in vivo analyses identified kaempferol 3-gentiobioside as an FXR partial agonist protecting against cholestatic liver disease
The Long and Lucky Road to Continuous Molecular Monitoring: A Personal History of Electrochemical Aptamer-Based Sensors
items.abstract: “Continuous molecular monitoring”, the ability to measure specific molecules in vivo, in real time, and at high frequency, could transform biomedical science and clinical practice. It could, for example, expose physiological dynamics that current “sample-then-analyze” paradigms obscure and improve the personalization of medical treatment, such as via feedback-controlled dosing that responds automatically to a patient’s changing physiology. Unlocking the full potential of continuous molecular monitoring requires a reagentless, reversible sensing mechanism both selective enough to deploy in the body and general enough to detect almost any analyte, a combination that had long proven elusive. Enzymatic sensors, for example, including the continuous glucose monitor, often work well in vivo but are limited to the small number of analytes for which suitably transforming enzymes exist. “Affinity biosensors”, in contrast, do not require the chemical transformation of their target, rendering them far more general. However, these have historically relied on adsorption to generate a signal (e.g., binding-induced changes in mass), a mechanism that performs poorly in unprocessed biofluids in vitro, much less in vivo. In this Account, I describe the near-30-year effort required to create and bring to clinical trials the first affinity biosensor architecture that performs well in vivo: electrochemical aptamer-based (EAB) sensors. To achieve this, EAB sensors use the binding-induced folding of an electrode-attached aptamer to alter the electron transfer kinetics of an attached redox reporter, a biomimetic signaling mechanism that is reagentless, spontaneously reversible, highly selective, and thus supports the real-time, in vivo measurement of almost any analyte for which a suitable aptamer is available. The road to EAB sensors began in the late 1990s with coincidentally convergent evidence suggesting that binding-induced folding is a near-universal property of destabilized proteins. Through the years-long contributions of many creative collaborators, this ultimately evolved into a nucleic acid-based, electrochemical biosensor architecture of broad utility. However, while even the first examples worked well in blood serum in vitro, EAB sensors drift when placed in the body, a problem ultimately solved by an engineering insight: the strongly frequency-dependent signaling of EAB sensors makes it possible to use them as their own drift-correcting reference. Leveraging this, in 2017, we demonstrated the first real-time, multihour in vivo monitoring of circulating drugs, an advance since extended to a wide range of analytes, to week-long in vivo operation and to feedback-controlled drug delivery. Given these unique measurement and control capabilities, EAB sensors can answer scientific questions and solve clinical problems that other technologies cannot. Seconds-resolved EAB sensor measurements are beginning to reveal, for example, previously unrecognized regulatory and clearance mechanisms and to reshape our understanding of drug and metabolite transport within the body, and the recent successful clinical trial of wearable EAB sensor “patches” supporting real-time measurements of the antibiotic vancomycin suggests the technology could similarly advance the measurement of drugs and biomarkers in healthcare. In short, I believe the continuous molecular monitoring that EAB sensors enable is poised to revolutionize our understanding of physiology and our ability to detect, monitor, and treat disease.

items.title: From Empirical Structural Modification to AI-Driven Design: Reinvigorating Natural Product-Based Medicinal Chemistry for Lead Discovery
items.abstract: data-centric era, dissect the specific bottlenecks embedded within traditional workflows, then examine AI-enabled lead discovery, analyze the inherent limitations of such approaches, and outline the community-level funding and resource investments required to enable their widespread adoption.

items.title: Alcimaterpenoids A and B, Two Enantiomeric Pairs of Bis-Denudaquinol-Monoterpenoid Meroterpenoids from the Endangered Plant Alcimandra cathcartii
items.abstract: Alcimaterpenoids A (1) and B (2), two pairs of racemic bis-denudaquinol-monoterpenoid meroterpenoids, were isolated and identified from Alcimandra cathcartii. Electronic circular dichroism (ECD) computations, GIAO 13C{1H} NMR (in conjunction with DP4+ probability analysis), and extensive 2D-NMR spectroscopic analysis techniques were used to determine their structures and absolute configurations. Structurally, compounds 1 and 2 are the first enantiomeric bis-denudaquinol-monoterpenoid meroterpenoids. Plausible biosynthetic pathways were briefly proposed. Compound (±)–1 exhibited moderate cytotoxic activity against the human PLC/PRF/5 cell line (IC50: 20.6 μM).

items.title: Discovery and Optimization of Novel HDAC/Proteasome Dual Inhibitors with Antitumor Activity in Solid Tumor Models
Lysine Side-Chain-to-Backbone Macroamidine Formation Reveals Activation-First YcaO Catalysis
items.abstract: YcaO enzymes use ATP to modify chemically inert peptide-backbone amides, but the order of catalytic steps has remained unresolved. Here, we characterize a minimal Lysobacter ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (RiPP) pathway in which the stand-alone YcaO LmaB sequentially forms two lysine side-chain-to-backbone macroamidine linkages in the precursor peptide LmaA, revealing a previously unrecognized mode of YcaO-catalyzed peptide cyclization. Bioinformatic analyses place this pathway within a broader class of macroamidine-containing RiPPs, collectively termed macroamitides, which also includes the antibiotic bottromycins. High-resolution LmaB–LmaA structures directly resolve an O-phosphorylated peptide-backbone intermediate coordinated by ADP and three Mg2+ ions and capture the first macroamidine together with O-phosphorylation at the second reaction site. These snapshots reveal iterative substrate repositioning within a single active site. A structure of LmaB H75A retains the O-phosphorylated intermediate but traps the intact lysine nucleophile in a nonproductive conformation, identifying H75 as the general base that activates and positions the lysine ε-amino group for attack. Alanine scanning further reveals extensive tolerance of both ring-forming sequences. Together, these data establish that backbone O-phosphorylation precedes nucleophilic attack, revise the prevailing YcaO mechanism, and provide a model for engineering peptide-backbone chemistry during macroamidine formation.

items.title: TfOH-Promoted C–C Cross-Coupling of Iodonium Ylides with Nucleophiles
items.abstract: 2-Naphthol and coumarin represent privileged scaffolds prevalent in bioactive agents and chiral catalytic ligands such as naproxen, warfarin, and (R)-(+)-BINOL. Hybridization of these two skeletons is a powerful approach to generate unreported molecular frameworks with unique activity. We herein describe a TfOH-promoted C─C cross-coupling of 2-naphthols and other nucleophiles with coumarin-based iodonium ylides, delivering a series of novel scaffolds. This transformation requires no metal catalysts, proceeding under mild conditions with good functional group tolerance. Gram-scale synthesis and multiple postfunctionalization reactions confirm the synthetic practicability of this methodology. The obtained hybrid molecules exhibit promising potential for further exploration in organic synthesis and drug discovery.

items.title: Honeybee (Apis mellifera) venom and its bioactive peptides tertiapin and apamin modulate the proteome of SARS-CoV-2-infected cells
items.abstract: The continuing emergence of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) variants highlights the need for host-directed antiviral strategies with specific molecular mechanisms. Honeybee (Apis mellifera) venom (HBV) contains bioactive peptides with immunomodulatory and membrane-active properties, yet their effects on SARS-CoV-2 infection remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we investigated the antiviral activity and proteomic impact of whole HBV and two venom-derived peptides, apamin (APA) and tertiapin (TERT), in human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2-expressing HEK293 cells infected with SARS-CoV-2 spike-pseudotyped lentiviral particles. Cell viability and membrane integrity assays showed that HBV, APA, and TERT exerted limited cytotoxicity at the tested concentrations. In pseudovirus infectivity assays, HBV displayed the strongest inhibitory effect, reducing viral infectivity to 61.3% at 2 μg/mL, whereas APA reduced it to 73.3% at 0.5 μg/mL, and TERT showed weaker inhibitory activity. Comparative nano-liquid chromatography matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization tandem mass spectrometry revealed treatment-associated remodelling of the host-cell proteome. A shared signature of 215 proteins across HBV-, APA-, and TERT-treated infected cells was enriched in binding and catalytic activity, translational proteins, metabolite interconversion enzymes, cytoskeletal proteins, and pathways linked to integrin, Wnt, interferon, and Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription signalling. Protein-protein interaction analysis highlighted functional clusters associated with cytoplasmic translation, viral mRNA translation, and the Sec61 translocon complex, with EFTUD2, EPRS1, and HSPA4 emerging as central hubs. HBV treatment additionally promoted immune-related and interferon-stimulated gene products, including factors involved in innate antiviral defence, cytoskeletal organization, ion transport, and membrane structural reinforcement. These findings suggest that HBV reduces SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus infectivity through a multifactorial host-directed mechanism involving antiviral signalling, cellular architecture, and proteostasis, supporting further investigation of bee venom-derived compounds as antiviral agents.

items.title: First Conjugates based on a Sigma Receptor Modulator and a Proteasome-Impairing Agent. Design, Synthesis and Exploratory Biological Evaluation in Cancer Cells.
items.abstract: Cancer cells rely on a finely tuned proteostasis network to cope with high metabolic and proliferative demands. Targeting this vulnerability through the simultaneous modulation of both Sigma receptors (SRs) subtypes (i.e. S1R and S2R) and proteasome function represents an attractive and unprecedented strategy for the development of potential anti-cancer agents. The connection between Sigma receptor signalling and proteostasis suggested the design of conjugates combining a SRs modulator scaffold with a scaffold able to reduce proteasomal activity in cells. Here, we report the design, synthesis and exploratory biological evaluation of four conjugates ( 15a-b and 16a-b ) obtained by linking RC-106 and IP24 through PEG-based spacers, varying the attachment site on the RC-106 scaffold and the linker length. These prototypes retained SRs affinity, with the site of derivatization on the RC-106 scaffold dictating subtype preference. In glioblastoma (GBM) cell lines (T98G and U87-MG) and multiple myeloma (MM) cell lines (RPMI-8226) the new compounds were markedly more effective than the parent compounds. The most potent analogue, 16a ( RC-241 ), showed an IC 50 of 1.66 μM in T98G cells after 72 h and retained activity in 3D U87-MG spheroids. The compounds did not inhibit the isolated 20S proteasome, yet induced dose-dependent proteasome impairment in intact cells, pointing to an indirect, cell-context dependent mechanism. Holotomographic live-cell imaging in T98G cells showed that RC-241 triggers cytoplasmic vacuolization and accumulation of misfolded proteins, a morphology consistent with paraptosis-like death driven by unresolved proteotoxic stress. These results provide the first experimental assessment of the in vitro anticancer activity of conjugates designed to combine SRs modulation with proteasome impairment, and identify RC-241 as a starting point for further investigation of proteostasis-directed strategies in GBM and MM.

items.title: Discovery and SAR Studies of Viral Processivity Factor 8 (PF-8) Inhibitors as Anti-Kaposi’s Sarcoma-Associated Herpesvirus (KSHV) Agents
items.abstract: Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) causes several malignancies, while current antivirals targeting viral DNA polymerase provide limited clinical benefit. Here, we explored the viral processivity factor PF-8, an essential cofactor of the viral DNA polymerase, as an alternative antiviral target. Guided by similarities between PF-8 and the bacterial β-clamp (DnaN), we synthesized and evaluated 54 derivatives of a hit compound. Screening in reactivated KSHV-infected cells identified several inhibitors with low-micromolar antiviral activity. Selected compounds directly interacted with recombinant PF-8, as demonstrated by SPR and MST, and induced its thermal destabilization. STD NMR and docking studies provided insight into the binding epitope and putative binding mode. The most promising compounds, 1 and 38, inhibited viral DNA replication and reduced ORF45 protein expression. SAR analysis identified the 4-tert-butylbenzenesulfonamide and N-benzylpiperazine motifs as important for activity. These results support the investigation of PF-8 as an antiviral target and provide starting points for further optimization.

items.title: Discovery of Potent Orally Active Plasmodium N -Myristoyltransferase Inhibitors Using Fragment-Linking Approaches
items.abstract: N-Myristoyltransferase (NMT) is an essential eukaryotic enzyme and an attractive potential drug target for parasitic infections such as malaria and leishmaniasis. Co-crystallisation of a high-throughput screening hit with P. vivax NMT identified a novel binding mode, and cooperative binding experiments with fragments identified synergistic improvements in potency and opportunities for fragment-linking. Optimisation of the torsional angle of fragment linkage through phenolic ether enabled the desired activity spectrum and selectivity profile, and examples were progressed to a mouse malaria model, resulting in the selection of IMP-1002 for further evaluation. This early lead compound was efficacious after oral administration in a SCID mouse model and is highly active against both blood- and liver-stage forms of the parasite. Finally, we discovered that highly potent human NMT inhibitors, including IMP-1088, could be generated by introducing an additional fluorine atom to further tune the torsion angle.

items.title: Fold-Stabilized Zn(II) Metallohelices Inhibit mTOR Signaling and Modulate the Tumor Microenvironment in Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma
items.abstract: Water-stabilized metallohelices based on labile metal ions remain rare because of hydrolytic instability. Here, we report the design and synthesis of a unique class of optically pure, water-soluble, glycosylated Zn(II) metallohelix diastereomers that exhibit exceptional hydrolytic stability and potent, stereochemistry-dependent antiproliferative activity against intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC). In an orthotopic, AKT/YAP-driven ICC mouse model, treatment with the lead compound Λ-7a produced significant tumor growth inhibition. Mechanistic studies revealed that treatment with Λ-7a induced cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, accompanied by suppression of PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway signaling and reduced phosphorylation of downstream effectors. In addition, Λ-7a treatment was associated with reduced vascular and stromal marker staining and increased CD8+ T-cell and macrophage markers within the tumor microenvironment. Together, these results establish fold-stabilized Zn(II) metallohelices as a new class of metallodrugs exhibiting potent anti-ICC activity, suppression of AKT/mTOR pathway signaling, and treatment-associated changes in vascular, stromal, and immune-cell markers within the tumor microenvironment.

items.title: Silver-Catalyzed Direct Oxo-alkylation of Azauracils with Tertiary Cycloalkanols via C–C Bond Cleavage
items.abstract: In this study, using low-toxicity and easily accessible aryl-substituted tertiary cycloalkanols as starting materials, the precise C–H functionalization at the C6 position of azauracils is efficiently achieved under silver-catalyzed conditions. This strategy features operational simplicity, a broad substrate scope covering aryl-substituted tertiary cycloalkanols and diversely substituted azauracils, and high compatibility with azauracil cores fused to pharmaceutical scaffolds, thus affording an efficient approach to expanding the structural diversity of azauracils.

items.title: A Pt(IV)-Cluster-Nanobomb for Concurrent Activation of Triple Programmed Cell Death Pathways: A New Effective Method to Overcome Cisplatin Resistance
items.abstract: Activation of single programmed cell death (PCD) pathway frequently contributes to the development of cisplatin (CP)-resistance. Herein, we designed and synthesized a series of carrier-free Pt(IV) nano-prodrugs designated CSPNPs (6aNPs−6dNPs). These prodrugs integrate three functional components into a single entity: CP as the core PCD-initiator; disulfide-cinnamic acid (CA) derivatives as amplifiers; and hydrophobic chains for self-assembly. Enriched in tumors via enhanced permeability and retention effect, CSPNPs cleave disulfide bonds and reduce Pt(IV) in high-glutathione (GSH) tumor microenvironment, depleting GSH and releasing active Pt(II) and CA-derivatives. This multi-pronged intervention blocks GSH-dependent cytoprotective hub and synergistically triggers p53-mediated apoptosis, GPX4-related ferroptosis and copper-driven cuproptosis. Compared with CP, the optimal 6bNPs gained 78.7% tumor inhibition in 4T1 xenograft-bearing mice, increased intratumoral Pt-content by 13.5-fold and alleviated systemic toxicity. This study establishes a viable paradigm beyond conventional CP-based chemotherapy and offers a generalizable strategy to enhance the inherent multi-pathway bioactivity of traditional chemotherapeutics.

items.title: Design, Synthesis, and Pharmacological Characterization of Novel Kappa Opioid Receptor Agonists via Isosteric Replacement Strategy for Inflammatory Pain
items.abstract: Pain management remains a critical challenge, with mu opioid receptor (MOR) agonists carrying significant risks of respiratory depression and addiction. Kappa opioid receptor (KOR) agonists offer a promising alternative, but centrally mediated adverse effects such as sedation and dysphoria limit their clinical utility. We synthesized 24 nalfurafine analogues via isosteric replacement of its furan side chain with diverse aromatic moieties. All compounds retained high KOR binding affinity and full agonist efficacy, with most displaying G-protein biased signaling. Compound 10, prioritized based on its pharmacological profile, was inactive in thermal nociception assays at doses up to 10 mg/kg, yet produced potent, KOR-mediated antinociception in the acetic acid writhing assay (ED50 = 0.009 mg/kg) and attenuated colonic hypersensitivity in a TNBS-induced colitis model of chronic visceral pain, without significant hypolocomotion. Pharmacokinetic studies identified compound 10 as a P-glycoprotein substrate with limited brain exposure, consistent with a CNS-sparing profile and preferentially peripheral activity.

items.title: Evaluating the Dimensionality of Molecular Ensembles Using Deep Neural Network Stochastic Autoencoders
items.abstract: Stochastic autoencoders (SAEs), which omit the Kullback–Leibler prior-matching term of variational autoencoders and are therefore suited to reconstruction rather than generative sampling, offer a nonlinear route to reducing the dimensionality of molecular ensembles, but their behavior across systems of differing size and flexibility is poorly characterized. Training SAEs on molecular dynamics trajectories of oxycodone, deca-alanine, crambin, a bromodomain–JQ1 complex, and HIV-1 protease, we find that reconstruction error plateaus at a system- and model-dependent latent dimensionality, that the effects of dropout and batch normalization are system-specific, and that SAEs yield more distinct clusters than principal component analysis (PCA) at very low dimensionality and reconstruct large data sets more accurately than the deterministic autoencoder CompressTraj at low dimensionality. With two to four latent variables, SAE reconstructions of crambin and HIV-1 protease are as accurate as PCA with 6–18 components, two latent variables span their leading principal subspace as well as 9–15 components, and a single SAE coordinate recovers the end-to-end distance of deca-alanine (R2 = 0.97, versus 0.04 for the first principal component), whereas PCA is more accurate at higher dimensionality and for the near-rigid bromodomain ensemble. Latent-space perturbations show that SAE latent variables encode nonlinear, position-dependent collective motions that vary across the learned manifold.

items.title: Structural Modification and Anti-inflammatory Evaluation of Deep-Sea-Derived Cycloheptapeptide Derivatives against Inflammatory Bowel Disease via NLRP3 Inflammasome Signaling Suppression
items.abstract: The NLRP3 inflammasome plays a central role in the innate immune response of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and its excessive activation drives the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and compromises intestinal mucosal barrier integrity. In this study, the natural cycloheptapeptide unguisin E (1) was identified through anti-inflammatory screening of a marine-derived molecule library. To improve its anti-inflammatory potency, 1 was employed as a lead compound for structural modification at the C-2 position of the indole moiety via Suzuki coupling, affording a series of cycloheptapeptide derivatives (2−40). Among them, CHNQD-01024 (12) significantly inhibited IL-1β release from the NLRP3 inflammasome in THP-1 and J774A.1 cell lines at 0.4 μM, exhibiting inhibition potency comparable to the positive control MCC950 at 2 μM. In the DSS-induced colitis mouse model, CHNQD-01024 significantly ameliorated systemic inflammation, mitigated colonic tissue damage, and restored intestinal barrier function at doses of 5−15 mg/kg, with efficacy comparable to the first-line clinical drug 5-ASA at 50 mg/kg. Mechanistic studies showed that CHNQD-01024 suppressed NLRP3 inflammasome-associated inflammatory signaling, accompanied by the inhibition of NF-κB signaling and ROS production, reduced NLRP3 expression, and impaired ASC oligomerization. Taken together, these findings identify CHNQD-01024 as a promising marine fungal-derived anti-inflammatory lead suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome-associated signaling.

items.title: Thiophene-Linked Nucleotide Analogues as Selective and Nanomolar Inhibitors of Plasmodial 6-Oxopurine Phosphoribosyltransferases
items.abstract: 6-Oxopurine phosphoribosyltransferases (HGXPRTs) are essential enzymes in the purine salvage pathway of Plasmodium parasites and attractive antimalarial targets. However, the high conservation of their active sites with the human homolog complicates selective inhibitor development. Here, we report thiophene-linked nucleotide analogues as potent and selective inhibitors of plasmodial HG(X)PRTs. Structure-based modeling and conformational analysis guided the incorporation of a rigid thiophene core to control the orientation of phosphate-mimicking groups. C5 sulfonyl substitution markedly enhanced potency, yielding low- to single-digit nanomolar inhibitors of Plasmodium falciparum HGXPRT (PfHGXPRT). Compound 66 emerged as a lead inhibitor (Ki = 7 nM), showing up to ∼3300-fold selectivity over the human enzyme. Compound 63 was the most potent against Plasmodium vivax HGPRT (Ki = 30 nM), highlighting species-dependent linker length effects. Cellular activity remained limited, emphasizing intracellular delivery and/or prodrug activation as key remaining challenges. These compounds establish a promising selective chemotype for further antimalarial development.

items.title: Discovery of Potent and Chemically Diverse PYCR1 Inhibitors with Distinct Binding Sites and Modes of Action
items.abstract: Pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase 1 (PYCR1) supports tumor growth, stress adaptation, and metastasis but remains an early-stage therapeutic target, with few potent inhibitors and limited knowledge of ligandable sites and modes of action (MoAs). We screened the ∼100,000-compound European Chemical Biology Library and a focused kinase inhibitor collection, identifying 119 validated inhibitors, including several with submicromolar potency and spanning diverse chemotypes. X-ray crystallography showed predominantly non-catalytic-site binding and revealed multiple ligandable regions, including a new pocket enabling covalent targeting of Cys262. At another allosteric site, ligand-induced displacement of Gln10 interfered with NADH binding. Potent PYCR1 inhibitors among kinase inhibitors displayed mostly mixed inhibition kinetics, with one exception acting as an NADH competitor. These findings establish PYCR1 as chemically tractable through diverse MoAs, substantially expand its inhibitor chemical space, and provide starting points for next-generation inhibitors and molecular probes to investigate PYCR1 in cancer-associated metabolic reprogramming.

items.title: Selective Fluorination Affords Hydrophilic Synthetic Glycoconjugates Stable In Vivo
items.abstract: Therapeutics based on native carbohydrates such as lactose often suffer from short circulation half-lives in vivo due to their rapid clearance from the bloodstream by hepatic C-type lectin receptors, which limits their therapeutic efficacy. A common counter-strategy is to develop structurally distinct glycomimetics by introducing aromatic substituents. However, these modifications often increase hydrophobicity and, in multivalent conjugates, may promote nanoaggregation in the bloodstream, adversely affecting their pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. In our conceptually distinct approach, strategic fluorine substitution in the native carbohydrate scaffold modulates pharmacokinetics while preserving high water solubility and bioavailability. The prepared highly water-soluble multivalent glycopolymers fluorinated at the 3′- and 4′-positions based on a biocompatible polyoxazoline scaffold exhibited circulation times comparable to the unmodified macromolecular carrier and substantially longer than native lactose-terminated analogues. We establish site-selective carbohydrate fluorination as a broadly applicable platform to improve the pharmacokinetic properties of soluble glycan-based therapeutics, useful for targeting biomedically important lectins, such as β-galactoside-binding galectins.

items.title: A Refined Search of SARS-CoV-2 Main Protease Inhibitors as COVID-19 Antivirals
items.abstract: MPI8 was among one of the first SARS-CoV-2 main protease (MPro) inhibitors with strong antiviral potency. Building on its peptidomimetic aldehyde scaffold, we retained the P2 3-cyclohexylalanine and P3 O-tert-butylthreonine elements, which support S2 binding, S-subsite engagement, and likely cellular permeability, and varied the S4/S1′ substituents and covalent warheads. SAR and co-crystal structures identified compact N-terminal carbamates or amides bearing cyclopropane, isopropyl, or trifluoromethyl groups as favorable S4 binders. Benzoxazole/benzothiazole-carbonyl groups and acyloxymethyl ketones were explored as S1′-engaging motifs, with one benzoxazole-containing structure confirming tight S1′ packing by crystal structure. Nitrile and 2-amino-2-oxyacetyl warheads provided viable alternatives to the parent aldehyde. Combining optimized S4 groups with alternative warheads or S1′ motifs yielded multiple inhibitors more potent than MPI8. Notably, MPI-131 showed an IC50 of 1.7 nM, strong antiviral potency, and CC50 of 60.2 μM, placing it among the most potent MPro inhibitors reported.

items.title: Discovery of XT1061, a HBV Capsid Assembly Modulator, as a Promising Therapeutic Candidate for Clinical Treatment of HBV Infection
items.abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) persists as a major unresolved infectious disease. Patients typically require lifelong administration of nucleos(t)ide analogs (NAs) or interferons but seldom achieve functional cure. Recent studies indicate that HBV core assembly modulators (CAMs), when combined with NAs and interferons, can more effectively reduce HBsAg in plasma, thereby facilitating functional cure. In this research, we discovered compound 39 (designated XT1061) through structural optimization of previously reported GLP-26, which exhibited potent anti-HBV activity in vitro (EC50 = 1.0 ± 0.1 nM). In the murine AAV/HBV model, XT1061 induced rapid reduction of HBV DNA and sustained viral DNA clearance throughout treatment. Notably, Combination therapy of XT1061 with pradefovir mesylate (PDV) exhibited significantly enhanced efficacy compared with monotherapy. Further preclinical evaluation and Phase I clinical trials (NCT06280534) confirmed that XT1061 possesses favorable drug-like properties and low safety risks. Collectively, XT1061 represents a promising anti-HBV therapeutic candidate, providing a viable strategy for the clinical management of chronic HBV infection.

items.title: 18F-Labeled 7-Azaindole-Based Radioligands for Imaging Colony-Stimulating Factor 1 Receptor in Glioblastoma
items.abstract: A series of 7-azaindole-based compounds were designed and synthesized as novel colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) ligands. Four potent ligands (IC50 < 40 nM) were radiolabeled with fluorine-18 via the 5-fluoroethoxy substituent on the 7-azaindole ring and evaluated comprehensively in rodents and U87MG glioma models. Among them, [18F]PLX6 (IC50 = 12.3 nM) showed modest brain uptake and rapid clearance in rats. Micro-PET/CT imaging resulted in clear visualization of both subcutaneous and intracranial orthotopic U87MG gliomas. Treatment with PLX3397 or PLX5622 significantly reduced tumor uptake, indicating specific binding of [18F]PLX6 to CSF1R. Ex vivo autoradiography at 30 min postinjection (p.i.) confirmed high tumor-to-brain ratio (10.14 ± 1.52) and specific binding of [18F]PLX6 to CSF1R. Metabolic analysis showed that intact [18F]PLX6 was the predominant radioactive species in tumors at 30 min p.i. These results support further evaluation of [18F]PLX6 as a promising PET imaging agent for noninvasive visualization of CSF1R expression in glioblastoma.

items.title: Structure-Based Design of Potent Pan-YTHDF Ligands
items.abstract: The reader proteins YTHDF1-3 recognize m6A-RNA in the cytosol. Here, we present a structure-based medicinal chemistry campaign that culminated in the pan-YTHDF inhibitor 34 (Kd = 0.14 μM for YTHDF2 by calorimetry), which is selective against YTHDC1 and YTHDC2. The high-resolution crystal structures of the complex of YTHDF2 with six members of the series validate the structure-based design. Using the structural information, we designed compound 31 (IC50 = 0.22 μM for YTHDF2) and a negative control, i.e., its methylated analogue 31b. The cellular thermal shift assay provides evidence of YTHDF2 target engagement in cells for inhibitors 34 and 31, while the negative control 31b is inactive. Compounds 34 and 31 inhibit the proliferation of the AML cell lines MOLM-13 and THP-1. The inhibition of the YTHDF readers by 31 increases the level and stability of the transcript of TNFRSF1B. This renders THP-1 cells more sensitive to TNF-α-induced toxicity.

items.title: From Artificial Intelligence Outputs to Medicinal Chemistry Decisions in Kinase Inhibitor Discovery: Evidence Boundaries, Resistance-Aware Design, and DMTA Learning
items.abstract: Kinase inhibitor discovery increasingly requires integrated decision-making that extends beyond biochemical potency. Selecting the next analogue, defining the assay package, evaluating structural hypotheses, anticipating resistance, and assessing developability collectively require evidence from distinct experimental layers. In this Perspective, we argue that the practical value of artificial intelligence-assisted drug discovery (AIDD) in kinase inhibitor programs should be assessed not by predictive performance alone but by whether computational outputs improve medicinal chemistry decisions that can be implemented and experimentally tested. We treat AI-supported outputs as testable hypotheses whose value is determined by their effect on analogue selection, assay prioritization, resistance panel design, and information gain across Design−Make−Test−Analyze (DMTA) cycles. Using resistance-focused examples from EGFR, ALK/ROS1/TRK, BCR−ABL1, and BTK, we illustrate how explicit evidence boundaries, validation gates, and falsifying experiments can guide redesign decisions and learning updates.

items.title: Discovery of 2-(Phenylamino)-6 H -pyrimido[5,4- b ][1,4]oxazin-7(8 H )-one Derivatives as Selective ACK1 Inhibitors with Immunomodulatory Effects Enhancing Anti-PD-1 Therapy for Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
items.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype with limited therapeutic options due to the lack of actionable targets. ACK1 contributes to tumor progression and immune evasion, representing a promising immunomodulatory target whose inhibition can potentiate anti-PD-1 therapy in TNBC. Herein, we report the discovery and structure−activity relationship (SAR) of 2-(phenylamino)-6H-pyrimido[5,4-b][1,4]oxazin-7(8H)-one derivatives as a new class of ACK1 inhibitors. The optimized compound 20l potently inhibits ACK1 (IC50 = 1 nM) and its autophosphorylation in TNBC cells. In vitro, 20l suppresses TNBC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion while inducing cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. In vivo, 20l not only directly inhibits TNBC cell growth but also remodels the immune microenvironment and activates systemic immunity. Combined treatment with 20l and an anti-PD-1 antibody produced a TGI of 95.7% without evident toxicity. Thus, 20l represents a promising ACK1-targeted therapeutic lead that warrants further investigation for the treatment of aggressive TNBC.

items.title: An Engineered Heavy-Atom-Free AIE-Active Type-I Sonosensitizer for NIR-II Imaging-Guided Sono-Immunotherapy of Hypoxic Tumors
items.abstract: The low oxygen dependence of the type-I sonosensitizers renders them promising agents for the treatment of hypoxic solid tumors. However, the rational design of heavy-atom-free type-I sonosensitizers with NIR-II emission remains challenging. Herein, a series of NIR-II heavy-atom-free sonosensitizers were synthesized. Among them, RBT-TPE02 exhibited pronounced aggregation-induced emission (AIE) characteristics, good NIR-II fluorescence, and efficient type-I reactive oxygen species generation under ultrasound irradiation. After nanoformulation, RBT-TPE02 NPs demonstrated notable type-I sonodynamic therapy (SDT) activity, which enabled efficient inhibition of tumor cells under hypoxic conditions and induced pyroptosis-associated immunogenic cell death upon ultrasound irradiation. In vivo experiments further confirmed that RBT-TPE02 NPs mediated efficient NIR-II imaging-guided SDT, resulting in effective tumor suppression and the activation of anti-tumor immune responses. This work presents a heavy-atom-free AIEgen engineering strategy that integrates NIR-II fluorescence, oxygen-independent type-I sonodynamic action, and pyroptosis-mediated immune activation in a single molecular platform for imaging-guided tumor therapy under hypoxia.

items.title: Discovery of Nivegacetor, an Advanced γ-Secretase Modulator, for the Treatment of Alzheimer’s Disease
items.abstract: Recent clinical data regarding amyloid-beta (Aβ) antibodies support the validity of reducing Aβ-amyloidosis or aggregated Aβ as a disease-modifying therapy for Alzheimer’s disease (AD). γ-Secretase (GS) remains an important target for the treatment of AD, and its pharmacological modulation, instead of inhibition, can deliver a safe treatment. Following extensive efforts to optimize the pharmacological and physicochemical properties (e.g., potency, selectivity, and solubility) of our previous clinical candidate, RO7185876, and to mitigate safety findings observed during advanced toxicology studies, we successfully identified RG6289 (nivegacetor). Herein, we report the comprehensive optimization process and the exploration of multiple chemical subseries that led to the discovery of the nivegacetor. Currently in Phase II clinical trials, nivegacetor is characterized by an improved safety profile and holds the potential to halt or delay amyloid accumulation and become an orally administered disease-modifying therapy for the treatment of AD.

items.title: Discovery and Structural Optimization of Elephantopus scaber -Derived Sesquiterpene Lactones as Covalent PRDX6 Inhibitors for Colorectal Cancer
items.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a highly aggressive malignancy, highlighting the need for therapeutic agents with distinct mechanisms of action. Natural products provide structurally diverse and biologically privileged scaffolds for anticancer drug discovery. Building on an anti-CRC germacrane-type sesquiterpene lactone scaffold (SC) isolated from Elephantopus scaber Linn., we identified PRDX6 as a covalent target using a biotinylated probe and covalent mass spectrometry, which revealed engagement of the catalytic residue Cys47. Structure-guided C6 functionalization with a 1,2,3-triazole motif afforded compound 1c, which showed enhanced PRDX6 binding, inhibited PRDX6 enzymatic activity, and promoted intracellular ROS accumulation, leading to potent anti-CRC effects. To improve in vivo developability, a morpholine hydrochloride prodrug, 6c, was designed and synthesized. Compound 6c displayed favorable pharmacokinetic properties, efficient systemic release of 1c, and significant antitumor efficacy in CRC xenograft models. This study establishes SC-derived sesquiterpene lactones as promising natural product-based covalent PRDX6 inhibitors for CRC drug discovery.

items.title: Aluminum-Based Metal−Organic Framework Nanoplatform Combines Chemo-Nanotherapy in an Intrahepatic Walker 256 Rat Tumor Model: Association with Glycerophospholipid Metabolic Changes
items.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treatment is severely limited by the low efficacy and drug resistance of current monotherapies. While nanocarriers for sorafenib (Sor) delivery have been explored, platforms that combine multimodal therapy and elucidate deep-seated anti-tumor mechanisms remain lacking. To address this, we engineered a nanosystem by loading Sor onto an aluminum-based metal−organic framework (Sor@Al-MOF), which combines chemotherapy with the intrinsic bioactivity of the nanocarrier. Sor@Al-MOF nanoparticles exhibited a well-defined lamellar structure, with a zeta potential of 10.10 ± 0.69 mV. Sor@Al-MOF achieved a high drug loading content (56.43% ± 0.36%) and encapsulation efficiency (77.38% ± 4.20%), and exhibited a cumulative release of 65.74 ± 0.55% at pH 5.3 after 72 h. In vitro, Sor@Al-MOF showed potent cytotoxicity against human HCC HepG2 cells (IC50 = 88.40 ± 0.12 μg/mL). In an intrahepatic Walker 256 rat tumor model, Sor@Al-MOF demonstrated enhanced therapeutic efficacy. Integrated metabolomics provided preliminary insights into potential metabolic changes in this model, including changes in choline kinase α (CHKα)-related glycerophospholipid metabolism. This study presents Sor@Al-MOF as a promising combinatorial nanotherapeutic candidate and offers a foundational basis for exploring metabolism-targeting strategies in liver cancer treatment.

items.title: End-to-End Prediction of Subcutaneous Peptide Absorption Rates from Amino Acid Sequences Using Physics-Informed Machine Learning
items.abstract: The subcutaneous (SC) absorption rate constant (ka) dictates critical pharmacokinetic and dosing parameters of injectable peptide therapeutics, yet currently, it cannot be predicted prior to clinical testing, forcing empirical decisions at the discovery and formulation stages. We address this important gap by constructing the first end-to-end machine learning framework that predicts SC ka, both point predictions and prediction intervals, purely from the amino acid sequence and conjugate chemistry. For developing the model, we first curated a comprehensive database of 41 human clinical ka values (0.0077−7.61 h−1), covering unmodified, fatty-acid-acylated, and protein-conjugated peptides. These data were subsequently encoded into a combination of protein language model (ESM-2) embeddings, chemical language model (ChemBERTa) embeddings, and 30 physics-informed molecular descriptors designed to capture the physical variables governing SC transport. Seven machine learning (ML) architectures and ensembles thereof were trained, with the best model (NGBoost) achieving R2 = 0.850 under leave-one-out cross-validation, a markedly high accuracy given the large variance in the clinically reported ka values. Notably, models trained on the physics-informed molecular descriptors or combinations thereof substantially outperformed models trained purely on learned embeddings (ESM-2, ChemBERTa)a direct consequence of the small scale of our training dataset. SHAP interpretability analysis indicates that predictions are consistent with established SC absorption physics, with properties including molecular weight, net charge, hydrophobicity, and acyl chain molecular characteristics dictating model predictions. Leveraging Jackknife+, the developed framework also reports ka prediction uncertainties (prediction intervals). Overall, this framework enables high-throughput sequence-level candidate ranking before in vivo data become available, supporting the rational early-stage development of peptide therapeutics.

items.title: Conserved recognition and divergent peripheral dynamics of designed statin analogues at human HMG-CoA reductase: ensemble docking and replicated molecular dynamics
items.abstract: Human 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A reductase (HMGCR) recognizes statins through a conserved polar binding region, while peripheral chemical differences may alter protein–ligand dynamics. We docked 13 chemically defined statin-related molecular states across six ligand-bound HMGCR crystal structures using three independent searches per state–receptor combination (234 searches). Eight selected states were then evaluated in three independently seeded 50 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations each (24 trajectories; 1.2 μs total). Protein-aligned root-mean-square displacement (RMSD) was analyzed for the entire ligand, a conserved nine-heavy-atom hydroxy-acid motif, and the complementary peripheral atoms, together with residue-level contacts. Top-ranked motif-compatible pose recovery varied between receptor structures, from 15/39 searches for 1HW8 to 38/39 for 1HWK. The G3-001 stereoisomers differed substantially in the persistence of geometric hydrogen-bond criteria involving HMGCR Glu559: median replica occupancies were 8.2% for G3-001 A (R) and 91.0% for G3-001 B (S), with higher occupancy for B in each of the three paired replica comparisons. A separate ether-chain extension (G3-005) exhibited pronounced peripheral displacement in one replica while selected recognition-site proximities remained. These computational observations identify testable relationships among receptor conformation, ligand stereochemistry, and interaction persistence.

items.title: Identifying Short Half-Life Compounds from Structure Information Using Multi-Task Graph Neural Networks
items.abstract: Accurate prediction of terminal half-life (t1/2) is paramount for prioritizing drug candidates during the lead optimization stage, as it minimizes the risk of clinical trial failure while optimizing resource allocation. Drugs characterized by suboptimal t1/2 profileseither excessively short or prolongedpresent significant challenges in dosage design and are frequently associated with increased risks of adverse effects. Traditionally, the determination of t1/2 has necessitated in vivo experiments to derive total clearance (CLT) and volume of distribution (Vss). In this study, we curated a comprehensive dataset of over 1400 compounds and developed deep learning-based regression models to predict t1/2 directly from molecular structures using Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). We implemented both single-task and multi-task learning architectures; the latter integrated CLT, Vss, and other related pharmacokinetic parameters to leverage their inherent physiological correlations. Our results indicate that a multi-task model achieved higher predictive performance than the single-task counterpart, with notably high precision in identifying compounds with short t1/2. By enabling the structural-based identification of unfavorable t1/2 profiles without the need for experimental data, this approach provides a robust and efficient tool for streamlining candidate selection in the early stages of drug development. This methodology is expected to accelerate the discovery of compounds with favorable pharmacokinetic properties, reducing the reliance on late-stage experimental validation.

items.title: Fe-Mediated Hydrofluorination of Piperidines: Access towards Fluorinated Iminosugars
items.abstract: Late-stage hydrofluorination provides access to fluorinated bioactive compounds suitable for 19 F NMR monitoring of biological processes. We report Fe(III)-mediated radical hydrofluorination of highly substituted, chiral N -heterocycles containing piperidine, indolizidine and pyrrolidine scaffolds to the Markovnikov products. This method tolerated steric bulky substrates as well as substituents on nitrogen with different electronic effects. Finally, an Fe(III) catalytic system was compared with Co(II) and Ni(II) catalysts.

items.title: Oxidative Nucleophilic Aromatic ipso-Substitution for the Late-Stage Functionalization of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons with Five-Membered Rings
items.abstract: Nanographenes and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are promising materials for advanced organic electronics, but their late-stage functionalization remains challenging. Here, we report an ipso-substitution, in which tert-butyl groups, which are usually installed for solubility reasons, are selectively replaced by mesylates on PAHs and nanographenes bearing five-membered rings. The reaction proceeds via an oxidative nucleophilic aromatic substitution mechanism and can be implemented in oxidative cyclodehydrogenation protocols to produce substituted PAH skeletons in one pot. Density functional theory calculations (DFT) support the suggested mechanism. Post-functionalization of the mesylates is possible according to literature-known protocols and is successfully demonstrated by the introduction of ether, alkyne, and aryl substituents. By controlling the amount of oxidant and the reaction time, the method enables the synthesis of asymmetric functional hydrocarbons from symmetric precursors overcoming statistical limitations by other protocols. Selected tert-butyl groups thus act as sites for the late-stage functionalization of nanographenes and PAH dyes.

items.title: Photocatalytic Cascade Acylative Cyclization of Phenyl-Bridged 1,6-Enynes with Acyl Oxime Esters: Access to Cyclopenta[ a ]indenes
items.abstract: All-carbon fused [6.5.5] tricyclic scaffolds are prevalent in natural products and bioactive molecules. We report visible-light-promoted cascade acylative cyclization of phenyl-bridged 1,6-enynes with acyl oxime esters, rapidly assembling diverse cyclopenta[a]indenes in moderate to good yields under mild photoredox conditions, with broad scope and functional group compatibility.

items.title: Lysine-Targeted Covalent Inhibition of eIF4E with an Anionic Electrophile Warhead
items.abstract: Covalent strategies offer a powerful route to expand the druggable proteome, yet selective lysine targeting remains difficult due to the high pKa and protonation of the amine side chain. The translation initiation factor eIF4E, an mRNA cap-binding protein that controls nuclear export and translation of oncogenic transcripts, has long been considered an undruggable RNA-binding protein. We apply an anionic electrophile strategy that converts a carboxylic acid within a reversible eIF4E ligand into a vinyl acylsulfonamide warhead, preserving salt-bridge and hydrogen bonding interactions in the cap-binding pocket and facilitating Lys162 deprotonation to enable site-specific engagement. This single-step transformation yields JL-03, a potent covalent eIF4E inhibitor with excellent stability toward biological nucleophiles, consistent with context-dependent activation of the warhead in the binding site. In cells, JL-03 achieves robust target engagement and suppresses translation of the oncogenic driver cyclin D. JL-03 reduces the viability of HOXA9-high acute myeloid leukemia cells with greater potency than reversible eIF4E inhibitors and synergizes with the menin inhibitor revumenib, demonstrating that coordinated transcriptional and translational blockade exhausts leukemic dependencies. These findings establish eIF4E as a tractable covalent target and highlight anionic electrophile installation as a generalizable strategy for lysine-directed covalent inhibitor design.

items.title: A Small Molecule Inhibitor of the Staphylococcus aureus agr Quorum Sensing System with Low-Nanomolar Potency
items.abstract: The accessory gene regulator (agr) quorum sensing system regulates virulence in certain common Gram-positive bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus. Small molecules that block agr have been reported, but most have modest potencies and warrant further mechanistic characterization. Herein, we report a structure–function study on CP-20, a compound recently shown to inhibit agr in S. aureus by targeting the histidine kinase AgrC. We designed a robust new synthetic route to the CP-20 scaffold, generated a collection of CP-20 analogues, and evaluated their activities in cell-based agr reporter and phenotypic assays. These investigations led to the discovery of a compound, CP-20t, which inhibits agr in S. aureus with low-nanomolar potency and acts on AgrC. CP-20t represents, to our knowledge, the most potent small molecule inhibitor of agr known—bridging the almost 1000-fold potency gap between peptide- and small molecule-based inhibitors—and is a powerful tool to study quorum sensing in S. aureus.

items.title: Electrochemical Insights into Histatin 5 Antimicrobial Activity: Cu(II) Redox Chemistry and Model Lipid Layer Interactions
items.abstract: Histatin 5 (Hst5) is one of the most potent antifungal members of the salivary histatin family, exhibiting activity against the opportunistic fungus Candida albicans, with reported intracellular localisation to mitochondria and effects on mitochondrial function. This localization, together with Hst5's ability to bind redox-active Cu(II) ions, suggested that Cu(II)-Hst5 complexes could catalyze ROS production via Cu(II)/Cu(I) cycling. The high stability of the primary Cu(II)-Hst5 complex engaging the ATCUN motif and its high resistance to the reduction call into question the feasibility of such a mechanism. Employing electrochemical methods and spectroscopic measurements, we investigated how copper coordination influences redox reactivity in Hst5 and its N-terminal fragments, examining two possible sources of redox activity in Cu(II)/Hst5 mixtures. The first involves either incomplete Cu(II) coordination within the ATCUN motif or Cu(II) ions not bound to Hst5. The second is the binding of excess Cu(II) to additional Cu(II)-binding sites in the Hst5 sequence. We also utilized electrochemical techniques to investigate the interactions of Hst5 and its Cu(II) complexes with DMPC-based lipid layers, revealing stronger perturbation by full-length Hst5 than by its N-terminal fragments.

items.title: Discovery of 2-((4-(phenylsulfonyl)piperazin-1-yl)methyl)-1H-indole derivative B9, an Anti-Inflammatory Agent Targeting Acute and Chronic Inflammation for the Treatment of Acute Lung Injury and Diabetic Kidney Disease
Next-generation antimicrobial platforms: integrating aggregation-induced emission for biofilm control
Auditing frozen chemical language model embeddings for drug-delivery screening: fingerprint baselines, random-initialization controls, and scaffold-memorization control tasks
items.abstract: Frozen embeddings from pretrained chemical language models (cLMs) are widely used as features for ADMET and drug-delivery prediction, often with a linear probe and little validation of what the representation actually contributes. We audit two small public cLMs (ChemBERTa-77M-MLM and ChemBERTa-77M-MTR, 3.4M parameters each) on three delivery-relevant endpoints from openly licensed sources: blood–brain barrier penetration (B3DB, CC0), PAMPA permeability (NCATS via PubChem), and Caco-2 permeability (OpenADMET, CC-BY-4.0). For each endpoint we compare frozen mean-pooled embeddings with (i) Morgan-fingerprint linear probes with train-only tuned regularization, (ii) the same architecture with random weights (five initialization seeds), and (iii) scaffoldconstant control tasks in the style of Hewitt and Liang that quantify how much a linear probe can score by memorizing scaffold identity. On observed means, tuned fingerprint probes are slightly ahead of frozen embeddings on all three endpoints (paired per-split differences of 0.016–0.032 in AUROC or R2, smaller than split-to-split variation); trained embeddings exceed random-initialization controls by 0.04–0.10; endpoint probes are selective above scaffold-memorization controls, and the memorization ceiling rises with layer depth in the primary MLM model. Decodability of bulk physicochemical descriptors (molecular weight, TPSA, fraction sp3, aromatic rings) is largely preserved under random initialization, indicating an architectural rather than learned origin for those signals; learned increments appear for logP, hydrogen-bond donors, and rotatable bonds. We quantify three practitioner pitfalls: pooling choice changes endpoint AUROC by up to 0.05; tuning the fin- gerprint baseline’s regularization changes it by up to 0.03 AUROC or 0.20 R2; and scaffoldsplit construction details change means by up to 0.04, exceeding seed standard deviations. The source datasets are public and cited; all curation scripts, pipeline code, and per-seed results are included in the accompanying package. The study is compute-bounded to CPU and small models, which limits the generality of the conclusions to that regime.

items.title: Integrating artificial intelligence and molecular simulation for peptide discovery: limitations, validation and decision-centered workflows
items.abstract: Summary. Therapeutic peptides occupy a chemical and pharmacological space between smallmolecules and biologics, offering extended recognition surfaces and access to targets that resist conventionalmodalities. Their discovery, however, requires the simultaneous optimization of activity, selectivity, stability, permeability and synthetic feasibility across a conformationally complex and chemically heterogeneous search space. Artificial intelligence (AI) andmolecular simulation address complementary aspects of this problem: AI learns structure–property relationships and explores large candidate libraries, whereas simulation interrogates conformational ensembles, target recognition and membrane-associated behaviour within an explicit physical model. We organize the field around a single, more discriminating question: under which chemical, biological and decision-making conditions does adding molecular simulation to an AI workflow improve peptide discovery outcomes enough to justify its cost? To answer it, we introduce a decision framework linking peptide chemistry and discovery endpoint to the decision beingmade, the uncertainty limiting that decision, the evidence that computation or experiment can provide, the cost of obtaining that evidence and the criterion for proceeding or stopping. Recent advances in biomolecular structure prediction, protein language models, generative design andmacrocycle engineering supply powerful enabling capabilities, but their transfer to short, flexible, cyclic and chemically modified peptides remains unevenly validated. Critically, a structured survey of 15 integrated studies shows that none (0 of 15) included a matched-budget comparison against an AI-only or conventional baseline, a scarcity we treat as a central empirical finding rather than an inconvenience. We outline reporting, benchmarking and prospective-validation standards by which genuine progress should be judged, and define what ‘developable’ must mean at the hit, lead and candidate stages.

items.title: Design and Benchmarking of CK2α′-Preferring Inhibitors for Huntington’s Disease: The Limits of Structure-Based Isoform Selectivity
items.abstract: Protein kinase CK2 acts through two catalytic isoforms, CK2α (A1) and CK2α′ (A2), whose ATP-binding sites differ at only two hinge positions, making isoform-selective inhibition difficult. We tested whether a standard structure-based pipeline can design and rank CK2α′-preferring compounds. In a paired benchmark of 140 compounds measured against both isoforms, none of the five docking-derived criteria, computed with GNINA and convolutional neural network rescoring, correlated with measured selectivity (ρ = −0.19 to +0.12), and for matched pairs differing by a single linker methylene, the scoring reversed the experimental order. The only reliable determinant of preference, a two-carbon linker within the benzo[c][2,6]naphthyridine scaffold, was obtained from the measured activities rather than from any computed score. Molecular-dynamics ensembles of the two isoforms overlapped (0.88 Å between versus 0.72–0.96 Å within), placing the selectivity signal below the resolution of the methods. From an enumerated series, EV043 showed the largest end-point free-energy preference for CK2α′ (ΔΔGb -7.74 kcal/mol), although this value remained sensitive to the starting pose in CK2α, while the non-selective inhibitor CX-4945 was reproduced correctly (+0.08 kcal/mol). Distinguishing CK2α′ from CK2α therefore requires alchemical free-energy methods supported by experimental validation.

items.title: Swapping O for S: Converting Oxetanes into Thietanes and their Oxidized Derivatives
items.abstract: Thietanes, often considered as “oxetane analogs”, offer complementary physicochemical properties and, along with their oxidized derivatives, are attracting increasing interest in medicinal chemistry. Their exploration, however, remains limited, partly due to the restricted availability and structural diversity of appropriate building blocks. The variety of methods available for preparing oxetanes with diverse substitution patterns makes their conversion into thietanes an appealing strategy for both building-block synthesis and late-stage diversification. However, existing O-to-S exchange methods mostly rely on the sulfurization of a 1,3-diactivated intermediate, require forcing conditions, and, importantly, provide very limited access to C(2)-substituted thietanes. We report herein a one-pot, two-step sequence for the mild and efficient O-to-S exchange in oxetanes. The approach relies on an autoactivation via a group-transfer strategy that bypasses the need for diactivated intermediates and provides access to thietanes with unprecedented substitution patterns, thus expanding the range of building blocks available for molecular design. Extensions to the formal O-to-SO, O-to-SO 2 and O-to-S(O)NH exchanges are also reported.

items.title: Mechanistic Monte Carlo assessment of colocalized permeation enhancement and efflux modulation for oral peptide delivery
items.abstract: The oral absolute bioavailability of 2- to 4-kDa peptides remains near 1%. We constructed a mechanistic Monte Carlo model of a colocalized, reversible permeation-enhancer and efflux-modulator architecture (Dual-Lock) with explicit mass balances and evidence-graded, correlated priors and asked when it would increase bioavailability to at least 4% with predicted reversible epithelial exposure. The arms shared random draws so that the ablations and negative controls isolated each component. Global sensitivity, benefit-risk and falsification analyses, spatial and uptake-constrained transport models, reversibility-endpoint scenarios, observation-conditioned analysis and an out-of-sample evaluation of an optimized design tested robustness. With the reference calibrated to 1.2%, Dual-Lock reached a median of 5.0% at half the enhancer dose and met the target in 45% of draws against 15% for the reference. Confinement caused most of the benefit: a matrix-only control gained 8-fold over peptide alone, from thinning the niche (3.3-fold) and the protease shield, and the gain survived stagnant-layer and solubility limits. In the uptake-constrained model success was 54% (reference 9%); it was 21% to 34% if the reference performs like oral semaglutide, and the upper tail stayed beyond published values. The advantage survived damage at the efficacious concentration but not below it. A credible release-rate optimum added 8 to 12 points out of sample. The transport structure is not independently validated; failure boundaries define the first experiments. Results are conditional on author-assigned priors.

items.title: Highly tunable artificial Suzukiase catalyzes the atroposelective synthesis of N -heterobiaryls
items.abstract: Enantiopure N -heterobiaryls are valuable motifs in medicinal chemistry and asymmetric catalysis. Yet, their atroposelective synthesis via Pd-catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling remains challenging as Lewis-basic heterocycles can coordinate to the Pd catalyst and inhibit catalysis. Herein, we report an artificial Suzukiase based on a biotinylated dialkylbiarylphosphine-Pd cofactor embedded within a streptavidin scaffold (Sav). Anchoring of the Pd cofactor minimizes unproductive coordination by N -heterocycles, enabling atroposelective cross-coupling of otherwise challenging heteroaryl substrates. Chemo-genetic optimization was achieved by screening six biotinylated dialkylbiarylphosphine ligands combined with a 400-member double-site saturation Sav library. The resulting Suzukiases catalyze the atroposelective synthesis of diverse axially chiral N -heterobiaryls, including (iso)quinoline, pyridine, pyrimidine, and other pharmaceutically-relevant heterocyclic scaffolds. Stereodivergent access to either atropisomer was achieved through variation of the protein scaffold and the Pd cofactor. This study highlights how an engineered protein environment can minimize substrate-induced catalyst deactivation while providing tunable stereocontrol in asymmetric Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling.

items.title: A Ligand-Centered Radical Reveals Orbital-Specific Bonding Differences Between Near-Isoradial Transuranium-Actinide and Lanthanide Complexes
items.abstract: Understanding how metal-ligand covalency evolves across the actinide series and compared to the lanthanide series remains a central challenge in f-element chemistry because subtle changes in both the energies and radial extension of the 5f and 6d orbitals can profoundly influence chemical bonding. Here, we employ a redox-active bipyridyl ligand platform to isolate trivalent actinide and lanthanide complexes of the form Cp* 2MIII(tBu2bipy•−) (1-M; Cp* = pentamethylcyclopentadienide; tBu2bipy•− = 4,4′-di-tert-butyl-2,2′-bipyridine radical anion; M = An = Np, Pu; M = Ln = La, Ce, Pr), including the second structually-characterized examples of Np and Pu complexes with organic radicals and the first examples with the metals in the trivalent state. Comparing their structural, electronic, spectroscopic, and electrochemical properties with those of the previously reported Am congener, 1-Am, and lanthanide counterparts 1-Nd and 1-Sm suggests a consistently greater degree of metal-bipyridyl bond covalency in 1-An relative to 1-Ln, which is reflected by shorter M–N distances as well as subtle ligand-based spectroscopic and electrochemical changes. Electronic structure calculations reveal that this enhanced covalency is driven by both increased σ-covalency—primarily involving the 6d orbitals in 1-An relative to 1-Ln—as well as ligand radical-to-metal 5f π-donation, which is absent in 1-Ln. Interestingly, the interplay of these bonding interactions leads to covalency trends that do not decrease monotonically across the actinide series. Instead, computational analyses suggest that while σ-covalency decreases across 1-An, π-covalency reaches a maximum in 1-Am before then decreasing again within a hypothetical curium(III) analog, 1-Cm. This energy-matching driven enhancement of 5f π-covalency amplifies otherwise subtle differences among ions with similar sizes and coordination preferences. More broadly, these orbital-specific trends across 1-An (Np–Cm) underscore the combined roles of spatial overlap and orbital-energy matching in soft donor radicalmediated actinide bonding.

items.title: Protein Tyrosine Phosphatase 4A3 (PTP4A3) as a Prognostic Biomarker and Pharmacological Target in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
items.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) represents a critical focus for biomarker research, given its high mortality, rapid progression, substantial treatment resistance, and marked genetic heterogeneity. The present study identifies PTP4A3 as a relevant molecular determinant in the disease, linking its overexpression to adverse clinical outcomes, genomic instability, activation of oncogenic signaling pathways, and the expansion of poorly differentiated myeloid populations. The integration of in silico analyses with in vitro functional assays demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of PTP4A3 significantly compromises leukemic cell viability and clonogenic potential, while promoting apoptotic signaling and reducing ERK1/2 phosphorylation in a time-dependent manner. The inhibitor JMS-053 showed consistent antileukemic activity across multiple AML cell models and displayed synergistic effects when combined with cytarabine, a cornerstone of current curative regimens. Collectively, these findings support the role of PTP4A3 as both a prognostic biomarker and a promising therapeutic target in AML, providing a rationale for further investigation of PTP4A3-targeted strategies in preclinical and clinical settings.

items.title: Two Approaches for the Conversion of Primary Sulfonamides to Sulfonyl Fluorides
items.abstract: This report describes two complementary methods for converting primary sulfonamides (RSO2NH2) into the corresponding sulfonyl fluorides (RSO2F). The first involves the copper-mediated fluorination of sulfonyl radicals generated photochemically from sulfonyl imines. This transformation leverages KF as the fluorine source and proceeds at room temperature under 390 nm irradiation. The second involves the electrophilic fluorination of sulfinate salts (RSO2–) generated via N-heterocyclic carbene-catalyzed deamination of primary sulfonamides. The reaction proceeds via a telescoped two-step sequence with initial formation of RSO2– followed by fluorination with N-fluorobenzenesulfonimide (NFSI) or SelectFluor. This latter transformation affords modest to high yields, including in the presence of unprotected anilines, carboxylic acids, and phenols, functional groups that are incompatible with many other methods for converting RSO2NH2 to RSO2F.

items.title: Discovery of N -Acyl Pyrimidine-Biphenyl Small-Molecule PD-L1 Inhibitors that Restore T Cell Function and Suppress Tumor Growth in Breast Cancer
items.abstract: The programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) is a promising target for cancer immunotherapy; however, no small-molecule inhibitors are approved to date. Herein, we designed and synthesized a series of N-acyl pyrimidine–biphenyl analogues as small-molecule PD-L1 inhibitors. Initial screening identified A6 and A12 as potent PD-L1 binders with EC50 values of 364 nM and 594 nM, respectively, in the luciferase reporter assay. The slightly superior activity of A6 was due to persistent binding with D122 during molecular dynamics. A6 also disrupted PD-1/PD-L1 interaction in an ELISA assay (EC50 = 15.21 μM). Functionally, A6 restored T cell activity, enhanced cytokine secretion, and promoted T cell-mediated tumor cytotoxicity. Importantly, A6 significantly suppressed tumor growth in a syngeneic 4T1 breast cancer model without any systemic toxicity, highlighting its potential to develop pyrimidine-based PD-L1 inhibitors for cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: Repurposing HIV Protease Inhibitors as Antifungal Chemosensitizers Against Multidrug Resistant Candida auris: Promise, Limitations, and Translational Challenges
items.abstract: Candidozyma auris (formerly known as Candida auris hereafter , C. auris ) is an emerging healthcare associated fungal pathogen. Which is associated with multidrug resistance, environmental persistence, and invasive infections in vulnerable patients. Reduced proneness to established antifungal agents has induced investigation of unorthodox strategies. One approach is antifungal chemosensitization, in which a compound with restricted or no direct antifungal activity enhances the effect of a prevailing antifungal. Preclinical studies have investigated chosen human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) protease inhibitors, including lopinavir, ritonavir, atazanavir, and saquinavir, in cooperation with azoles or amphotericin B against C. auris . Reported findings include in vitro synergy, enhanced fungal killing, and reduced fungal burden in experimental infection models. Intended clarifications include altered drug efflux and changes or modifications in cellular physiology, but the underlying/fundamental mechanisms remain incompletely established. Significantly, limitations include combination and isolate dependent effects, use of selected strains in some infection models, incomplete pharmacokinetic and toxicity data, and no demonstrated clinical efficacy. This Perspective evaluates the evidence and determines the independent validation, exposure response studies, drug interaction assessments, and safety studies needed before clinical application can be considered.

items.title: On-Demand Drug Release under Ultrasound Irradiation
items.abstract: Achieving precise, on-demand release of therapeutic agents remains a central challenge in pharmacology and chemical biology. In this work, we reported a modular prodrug release platform that employed low-intensity medical ultrasound (1 MHz, 2.5 W cm–2) to trigger the cleavage of carbamate and thiocarbamate linkers in aqueous media, enabling on-demand release of hydrophilic drug payloads. The linker was designed to couple drug release with the concurrent release of methylene blue (MB), allowing fluorescence measurements to track ultrasound-triggered linker cleavage and cargo release from the same molecular construct. Mechanistic studies including radical probes, EPR spectroscopy, Fenton validation, and intracellular DCFH-DA imaging supported the crucial role of cavitation-generated •OH and O2•– for the cleavage of the linkers. Furthermore, we evaluated payload compatibility using topotecan (TPT), an FDA-approved anticancer drug, and N-acetyl-l-cysteine as representative hydroxyl- and thiol-containing prodrugs, respectively. Ultrasound irradiation triggered TPT release and restored the cytotoxic activity of the masked prodrug in HeLa cells, whereas the nonactivated prodrug maintained >86% MCF-10A cell viability. Ex vivo studies also showed that ultrasound-triggered MB and TPT release remained detectable through porcine tissue barriers of 2.0 cm thickness, enabling controlled drug release with fluorescence-based monitoring and tissue-penetrating delivery.

items.title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Viral Nanobody Epitope Prediction
items.abstract: Rapid development of therapeutics against emerging viral pathogens increasingly depends on machine learning (ML), both to generate candidate binders and for structural validation. Nanobodies (Nbs), or single-domain antibodies, are promising antiviral therapeutics, but accurate in silico prediction of viral epitopes remains challenging. Here we benchmark three ML-based structure prediction models, Boltz-2, Chai-1 and AlphaFold3 (AF3), against a curated data set of viral antigen-nanobody complexes deposited after the AF3 training cutoff. AF3 outperformed the other models: success (interface DockQ > 0.23) rose from 33% with a single seed to 50% and 65% with 10 and 100 seeds-per-target, respectively, compared with 18% for Boltz-2 and 30% for Chai-1. Using an expanded data set, we evaluated confidence metrics and found that a strict ipTM cutoff of 0.8, or a combination of ipTM ≥ 0.6 with a CDR3 loop pLDDT ≥ 60, reliably excluded incorrect predictions while retaining most successful ones. We further establish best practices for two AF3-specific capabilities, the choice of antigen multimeric state and the inclusion of N-glycosylation, both of which can be decisive for epitope success depending on the target. Finally, we apply these guidelines to two design problems: ranking a library of VEEV-neutralizing nanobodies and mapping the epitope of the broadly neutralizing nanobody CC3 across homologous alphavirus antigens. These results provide a practical framework for ML-based viral nanobody epitope prediction and design.

items.title: Design, synthesis and biological evaluation of pyrazolo[3,4-d]pyrimidine derivatives as PI3K/HDAC dual inhibitors
What Method and Library Size Is Best for Fragment Screening?
items.abstract: Fragment screening is widely used to provide useful starting points for drug discovery. There are many methods that are used today for conducting fragment‐based screens. and fragment libraries vary widely in size. In this perspective, I discuss the method that I use for fragment screening and the size of my fragment library, the reasons for these choices, and provide an example that illustrates the advantages.

items.title: Amino Acid Functionalization Influences the Binding of Thiophene‐Vinylene‐Benzothiazolium‐Based Fluorescent Ligands to Protein Deposits in Tissue Sections With Alzheimer’s Disease Pathology
items.abstract: Detecting and distinguishing between structurally diverse protein aggregates involved in various neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD), remain key challenges in the development of molecular imaging tools. Recently, bi‐thiophene‐vinyl‐benzothiazoliums (bTVBTs), a class of thiophene‐based optical ligands, were synthesized and shown to enable selective labeling of tau pathology in AD brain tissue. Building on this framework, we report here the design and evaluation of a novel series of bTVBT ligands functionalized with L‐amino acids (glycine, alanine, valine, tyrosine, or glutamate) to explore their influence on ligand–filament interactions. When applied to sporadic AD brain tissue sections, the ligands displayed preferential binding to tau deposits when using 100 nM ligand, whereas all ligands bound to both amyloid‐β (Aβ) and tau aggregates at higher concentrations. The glycine‐functionalized bTVBT scaffold demonstrated the strongest fluorescence upon binding and was labeling all types of tau inclusions present in sAD brain tissue, whereas the glutamate‐functionalized ligand was the least potent. Thus, the chemical nature of the amino acid influenced the binding mode of the ligand to protein deposits. The observed trend in the ligands’ binding mode to the protein aggregates could also be correlated with distinct solvatochromic effects, indicating that certain amino acid side chains interfere with favorable interligand π–π stacking, thereby reducing binding specificity. Collectively, these results pinpoint that minor chemical alterations of the bTVBT scaffold influence the binding mode of the ligands to protein deposits, and we foresee that our findings will aid in designing ligands targeting proteinaceous aggregated species in AD and related neurodegenerative diseases.

items.title: Tandem Cyclization–Ring Opening of Chromenylamidines: A Direct Route to Pyrido[2,3‍‐‍d]pyrimidin‐4(1H)‐Ones With Anticancer Activity
items.abstract: Pyrido[2,3‐ d ]pyrimidinones can be considered privileged heterocyclic scaffolds as they are present in a diversity of molecules with a wide range of biological activities. This work describes a novel synthesis of pyrido[2,3‐ d ]pyrimidin‐4(1 H )‐ones from chromenylamidines by a cascade cyclization–ring‐opening reaction, induced by acetic acid catalysis and heating in ethanol. Preliminary biological evaluation identified several derivatives with significant and selective cytotoxic activity for triple‐negative breast cancer cell lines (low micromolar EC 50 values). This methodology provides a straightforward approach to 1,5,7‐triarylpyridopyrimidinones from readily available 4 H ‐chromene precursors, enabling access to a library of compounds with promising cytotoxic activity in cancer cell models.

items.title: His-tag-binding DNA aptamer–JQ1 conjugates enable comparative in vitro profiling of BRD4 ubiquitination
Green and Scalable Supercritical Fluid Chromatographic Resolution of 5-Nitroindoline Derivatives: Enantiomer-Specific Biological Evaluation and COX-2 Inhibition Insights
Direct-to-Biology High-Throughput Optimization Enables Rapid Hit-to-Lead Discovery of Potent CDK2 Inhibitors
Trifunctional zirconium catalysis-enabled triple modular synthesis
items.abstract: While zirconium catalysis has been predominantly confined to Lewis acid and redox applications in homogeneous synthesis, its potential in photocatalysis—particularly in C–H activation—remains largely unexplored. Here, with the demonstration of photoinduced inner-sphere α-homolysis (ligand-to-metal charge transfer) in zirconium catalysis, we report a trifunctional zirconium catalytic system synergistically integrating photochemical, Lewis acid and redox catalysis for triple modular synthesis from alkanes, aldehydes and nitriles, rendering structurally diverse benzylamines (up to 98% yield) and their deuterated analogues under mild conditions. Mechanistic studies validate a multifunctional catalytic cycle combining ligand-to-metal charge transfer-initiated radical chemistry with a ZrIV-mediated carbocation pathway. The protocol’s synthetic power is showcased through late-stage diversification of bioactive compounds, streamlined drug analogue synthesis, direct valorization of gaseous alkanes and gram-scale production with 100% atom economy. Zirconium catalysis has remained largely confined to Lewis acid and redox chemistry, with only isolated examples of photocatalytic C–H activation.
